en: The Ayurvedic Series of Texts.
The First Chapter, composed by the Venerable Upādhyāya Mādhava:
[Salutation] to the Sun, who causes the lotus-pond of the manifestation of meaning to bloom.
I take refuge in the body of Śiva and Śivā, which is the manifestation of existence, consciousness, and bliss. || 1 ||
May the dust from the lotus-feet of Heramba, reddened by contact with the Mandara-like crest-jewels of the Lord of the Gods, enter into our hearts.
Now we shall explain the purification of the king of essences (rasarāja), having examined various tantras, for the sake of the success of physicians. (3)
We indeed make an effort to reveal those very *saṃskāras* which are desired as dependent on others, hidden, and indicated by the perfected ones (*siddhas*). (4)
From this work, they extract ritual applications and insert their own names within its body;
may the lifespan of those who blacken their lineages with the heat of my labor come to an end. (5)
I do not write that which, though existing in the branches of the scriptures, was not composed by the mouth of the most learned Aṃśu.
I shall here relate that deed which I performed before my elders; for who would hesitate to recount his own exploits?
Those who are capable of teaching and bestowing the essence of the scriptures are indeed the gurus;
those who place themselves before such gurus are the true disciples.
The remaining [dramas], moreover, partake of the representation of both of these. || 7 ||
1. Consisting of the water-lily of dissolution, it is the sky (*khaca*). 2. Indicated by success, it is the sky (*khaca*). 3. Those who cast [it] down... 4. Having tasted it... 5. In detail...
Whatever was done by me, and whatever could be caused to be done—that work of the Lord of Sūtas has here been made manifest.
Those who teach this do not cause it to be performed; those who perform it do not study it—both of these have false purposes.
The rites that produce auspicious results are of many kinds; they are similar in being accomplished through effort that is either slight or great.
If you ask me to describe among them that which is easiest to perform—
What fruit is there for others from the utterances [of these mantras] beyond that? 9.
Whatever action is impossible to accomplish, whatever medicine is difficult to obtain—
all that having been abandoned, the essence is the three-fold fast (traikāśita).
In some branches there is no ritual action, nor is there any mention of the number of mantras; in some there is no application of rasa, and in some there is no tradition at all. (11)
Success is not found everywhere, whether in alchemy or in elixirs, nor in medical theory or its practical application; therefore, I have exerted effort [in this work]. || 12 ||

Whatever has emerged from the mouth of my guru and whatever has been personally experienced by me—desiring to benefit the hearts of people, I shall speak that very thing, free from contradiction with the scriptures. (13)

What exists elsewhere is found here; what exists here is found nowhere else—except for the single physician Rasu, who gains profit, honor, and fame. What physician could obtain even a single cowrie shell in exchange for grass, wood, and herbs? (14)

As long as the mercury (sūta) is not purified, nor dead, nor rendered unconscious, nor bound by fragrance (gandhabaddha), nor killed by the thunderbolt (vajra-mārita), nor killed by the sky (gaganavadha), and as long as the upasrutās are not pure;
and as long as the iron has not been struck by the sky-mercury, nor the poison, nor the clarified butter, nor the oil-cooking has taken place— [the elixir is not accomplished].

First, how does a physician become accomplished and worthy of praise within the circle of those who enjoy wealth? [The following] has been extracted... [the sequence-number]. Because of that, there is no success therein. [This was] known from his own mouth. It is now being made manifest. That something... Now, the defects of mercury (rasadoṣāḥ).
The serpent, the forest, impurity, fire, fickleness, and this mountain—these defects, along with the unbearable heat of fire, reside naturally in mercury (pārada). (16)
From dullness (jāḍya), there is leprosy (kuṣṭha) on the body; from impurity (mala), there is disease from the limbs;
from the heat of fire (vahneḥ vīrya), there is destruction of vigor; and from fickleness (cāpalya), death from poison (viṣa).
Even the bursting of a mountain arises from the fault of non-endurance; delusion is likewise born [from it].
These three—bile, wind, and phlegm—are the primary faults. (18)
In the rasa [metal], death, feverish distress, and fainting are the causes [of these defects] respectively.
The two [metals] produced by yoga, namely lead (nāga) and tin (vaṅga), bestow numbness, flatulence, and leprosy. 19.
Furthermore, seven other adventitious coverings (kañcukas) are proclaimed:
those born of the earth, those born of the mountain, those born of the wind, and two each born of the serpent and of tin. (20)
These twelve defects in mercury have been declared by those expert in the properties of mercury:
that which is born of earth causes leprosy, and that which is born of stone causes dullness of the senses. (21)
Mercury produced from water is rich in the aggregate of wind (vāta), while that produced from lead and tin is rich in defects (doṣa).
Therefore, for the sake of removing these defects, mercury should be purified with great effort. || 22 ||
When the king of essences has been purified and is free from defects, it bestows results equal to nectar;
when the mercury is thus devoid of faults, it removes both death and old age. (23)
Even this nectar, though it is directly immortal, is poison when possessed of defects;
therefore, for the sake of removing those defects, one must be accompanied by skillful physicians.
Having gathered all the necessary equipment, one should perform the alchemical process (rasakarma).
At an auspicious time, the mercury (rasa) should be taken in a quantity of exactly one hundred palas.
The supreme refinement of mercury should not be performed when it is less than fifty, twenty-five, ten, five, or even one *pala* in weight. (26)
Since the fruit that arises from what is accomplished with great effort is indeed small, one should worship the venerable Guru, the maiden, the young ascetic (baṭuka), and the Lord of the Gaṇas. (27)
Having first offered oblations to the Yoginīs and the Kṣetrapālas in four ways, he should then,
at an auspicious moment during the strength of the moon, enter the secret dwelling.

On an auspicious day and under a favorable lunar mansion, he performed the purification of the mercury; having washed and worshipped the mercury with the Aghora mantra, he then properly carried out the subsequent refinements, beginning with heating.
‘Aghorebhyo ’tha ghorebhyaḥ’ and so forth is a Vedic mantra.

A mortar made of iron is excellent; therefore, that which is produced from the essence [of iron] is superior. That which is made of magnetite (kāntaloha) is better than that, and likewise, one made of *madaika* is of the same kind.
In the absence of an iron mortar, one made from a smooth stone is auspicious;
it should be provided with a similarly clear and smooth pestle. || 31 ||
The eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) are sometimes considered nineteen; the number of the king of essences (rasarāja) is stated as eight in some places, while in others it is held to be nine.
Just as there is scratching, followed by rubbing and fainting, so too there arise rising, falling, obstructing,
and restraining; here, there is inflaming and the swallowing of the sky.
Following that, there is the movement of the second [power] situated within the womb. || 33 ||
The external procedure consists of: the second stage [duti], the digestion of the *sūtaka*, the "eating" (*khāda*), the "passion" (*rāga*), and then the process of *sāraṇā*;
followed by transference (*saṃkrāmaṇa*), the method of piercing (*vedha*), and the application to the body (*śarīrayoga*)—thus, the procedure here is eighteenfold. (34)

From the *Rasapaddhati*: Exhaustion, intoxication, fainting, and recovery; then the varieties of awakening, obstruction, restraint, and stimulation—thus the eightfold refinement is clearly established.

Other tastes are not included in this treatise because they are not useful for the subject at hand, or else due to a fear of prolixity, since all tastes are already applicable through their inclusion within the category of the salty taste. //35//
Vāgbhaṭa also says:
"Thus, these eight purificatory processes for mercury are equal [in importance] regarding substances used for rejuvenation (rasāyana);
the remaining ones, because they are useful for [ordinary] substances, are not employed by physicians. (36)

Now, the nineteen purificatory processes (*saṃskāras*): namely, sweating (*khedana*), rubbing (*mardana*), piercing (*vedhana*), raising (*utthāpana*), falling (*pātana*), awakening (*bodhana*), restraining (*niyamana*), inflaming (*saṃdīpana*), oiling (*anuvāsana*), the measure of the swallow of the ether and so forth (*gaganādigrāsapramāṇa*), moving (*cāraṇa*), internal melting (*garbhadruti*), external melting (*bāhyadruti*), alchemical digestion (*yogajāraṇa*), coloring (*rañjana*), extracting the essence (*sāraṇa*), transmutation (*krāmaṇa*), piercing (*vedhana*), and refining (*bhakṣaṇa*). These nineteen purificatory processes grant success in alchemy (*sūtasiddhi*); alternatively, the eight purificatory processes ending with inflaming (*saṃdīpana*) grant success in bodily perfection (*dehasiddhi*).
Now, among these, the procedure for sweating (*khedana*): [The text continues with the detailed ritual instructions.]
One should fill a vessel with various grains that have been husked and moistened with water, and preserve it until it reaches a state of acidity.
In the midst of that [are] ghanavāyu, uṇḍī, viṣṇukrāntā, punarnavā, mīnākṣī, sapakṣī, sahadevī, and śatāvarī. || 38 ||

Having ground together triphalā, girikarṇī, haṃsapādī, citraka, and the roots and stalks of śigru, one should add them as available into a previously prepared vessel of sour gruel; this becomes *dhānyāmlaka*. One should employ this "king of mercury" (*rasarāja*) in all processes such as sweating (*khedana*).
Or one should employ fermented rice gruel (māranāla) that is very sour; in its absence, one should use that. || 40 ||

Ghana is mustā; vāk is brāhmī; some read "bhaḍurāmuṇḍī" in its place—muṇḍī is well known; viṣṇukrāntā is the white-flowered aparājitā; punarnavā is called "gandhapūrṇā" in the vernacular; matsyākṣī is mīnākṣī, known as "machechī" (also "hum̐nagudā") in the vernacular; sarpākṣī resembles a snake's eye and is called "cucī" in the vernacular; sahadevī is well known; śatāvarī is called "śatāvarī" in the vernacular; triphalā is well known; girikarṇī has blue flowers.

*Aparājitā* is indeed *haṃsapādī*, also known as *haṃsacaraṇā*. *Citraka* is well-known. "With roots and stalks" means with roots and branches; "as available, exceeding half the number" is the convention of the Guru.
1. [The ingredients] should be ground together with their roots. 2. *Ulaguṇḍā* is mentioned in manuscript *kha*.
Tryūṣaṇa, salt, rājī, garlic, triphalā, fresh ginger, mahābalā, nāgabalā, meghanāda, and punarnavā. (41)
One should combine equal parts of Meṣaśṛṅgī, Citraka, and Navasāra, each added separately in a quantity equal to one-sixteenth part of the mercury. (42)
One should grind all these together, or individually, with sour gruel;
then, one should smear a cloth to the thickness of a finger with that paste.
One should place the bound mercury into the middle of that and cook it for three days.
When subjected to a swinging motion combined with sour substances, the mercury becomes exhausted. || 44 ||

Meghanāda is a variety of *taṇḍulīya*, a specific leaf-vegetable known in the vernacular as 'cavalāī'; *śṛṅgī* is *meṣaśṛṅgī*, and in its absence, *karkaṭaśṛṅgī* should be taken; *naksāra* is *navasāgara*, a specific type of alkali.
Now, another established view:
the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), salt, *asuyā*, *citraka*, and the roots of *ārdraka*.
Having been ground and strained, it should be repeatedly steamed with sour gruel (kāñjika) for three days. || 45 ||

Tryūṣaṇa is the three pungents (ginger, black pepper, and long pepper); lavaṇa is rock salt (saindhava); āsurī is rāī (cumin); citraka is well-known; ārdraka is śṛṅgavera (fresh ginger); mūlaka is the white radish, known in the vernacular as ‘mulī’. Having smeared the bark with the paste of these, and so forth, as described previously. The word *muhur* means every day, implying the application of the paste daily. Now, another established method: "Having bound the mercury in a cloth within a decoction of four times its quantity of vinegar (*kāñjika*), along with the pastes of the two excellent [pungents] and *vahni* (citronella), one should cook it using the *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus). (46)
Vyoṣa is the three pungents (trikaṭu); varā is triphalā; vahni is citraka; kanyā is the plant known in the vernacular as 'kuvārī', and its inner core should be taken.
Furthermore:
one should add each substance separately in a sixteenth part of the mercury's weight.
For substances whose measurements have not been specified, this measurement is held by the wise to be the standard. || 47 ||
If one is unable to remove the impurities over three days, one should continue to heat the king of essences (rasarāja) for one more day continuously, but with a fire that is not excessively intense.
Some, however, desire exhaustion preceded by rubbing; they are devoid of knowledge regarding the underlying rationale, and the contradiction of the sequential order is a flaw in their view.
Now, as for rubbing:
the physician should rub [the patient] with powders mixed in a sixteenfold proportion.
With the strained garments of the clarified butter and with the liquids and other substances to be described [in verse 49].
Having added the powder of house-soot and bricks, as well as curd and molasses,
along with salt and asafoetida, one should pour in the strained liquid and churn it thoroughly.
Just as a worn-out cloth, a decayed seed, and likewise mercury, when crushed bit by bit, absorb the dyes through the process of *nimela*. || 51 ||
Now, another established view:
it should be soaked repeatedly for three days with red brick, lampblack, the essence of *sāroṇī* smoke, and *khacūrṇaka*, combined with the juice of *jambīra*.
Alternatively, the mercury becomes supremely pure after being rubbed for even a single day;
one should then repeatedly collect it using an upward-pressing apparatus (ūrdhvapātanayantra).
Or from the stretching of the cloth, or from washing it with an alkaline solution.
Now, [the following is] for the cure of fainting: house-lizard destroys impurity; triphalā destroys digestive fire. (54)
It destroys the poison of the *citramūla* plant; therefore, one should diligently mix it with water, grind it, and cause it to faint [its potency] by repeating this seven times. (55)

Thus, when thoroughly processed and melted, it becomes free from defects; one should cause all metals to undergo this process of solidification (mūrchana), as prescribed in the science of alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), but not in the case of mercury (*rasa*). 56.
Now, another opinion is as follows:
One should massage the king’s face with the root [of the plant] together with a maiden, for the purpose of removing the defect of impurity; the massaging and the subsequent rising are auspicious.
To eliminate volatility, one should repeatedly perform the processes of rubbing and raising the king of minerals (mercury) with the juices of *kṛṣṇadhatūra*.
For the pacification of the defects of poison, one should use the water of Triphalā and Kanyakā;
for the defect of the mountain, one should diligently use Trikaṭu with the water of Kanyakā.
The destruction of fire [poison] is achieved with the powder of *citraka* and *kanyā*;
one should purify each respective humor (*doṣa*) with warm *āranāla*.
Thus purified, flowing, and free from the seven defects, it becomes the creator of the body; otherwise, it is incapable of performing its function.
Now, the removal of the impurities from mercury:
with a decoction prepared from maiden-hair grass (*kumārikā*), *citraka*, red lac, and mustard seeds, mixed with *ghuḍhṛtī*.
Even when the rasa is crushed with the three fruits, it is freed from impurities after three days. || 62 ||
Thus is the simultaneous destruction of all impurities.
Now, the process of raising [the mercury]:
Then one should raise the mercury, which has been treated with lime-juice, in the sun.
The powder remaining from the raising process should then be placed in a *pātana* (sublimation) apparatus.
Having heard this, the physician should collect the pārada (mercury) from the vessel that has not been covered.
Vāgbhaṭa also says:
"After this purgation, the purified *rasa* (plasma) must thereafter be protected."
Once it has been lifted up, it should thereafter be washed with sour gruel (kāñjika).
The *Rasaratnākara*, unable to endure the difficulty of [the process of] *utthāpana* (revitalization), describes an easy method as follows:
"Having washed it with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should take the ash and grind it;
having washed it again with sour gruel itself, one should take that and cause it to dissolve. (66)
Thus ends the method for the *lugama* [purification].
It is also stated elsewhere:
"By washing with water or with warm *aragvadha* juice, one shall arise [from the affliction]."
"Or else, one may arise from the *pātanā* [practice] at the *pātanā-yatra*. Thus [it is said].
Now, as for *pātanā*:
it is threefold, according to the divisions of upward, downward, and horizontal. Among these, the upward *pātanā* is as follows:"
Three parts [of the powder] are from *arka*, one part from *rasakha* (mercury), and then one part from *nimbuka*.
One should crush this until it attains the consistency of a ball;
then, one should place that ball in a lower vessel and pour water into an upper vessel.
Having prepared a basin and placed a wet cloth over it by someone, one should seal the fire beneath it and awaken it after four watches (twelve hours). || 70 ||
Then, one should take the mercury caught in the upper vessel by means of a mechanical device;
this is called "upward sublimation" (ūrdhvapātana) by physicians for the purpose of purifying the flowing [mercury]. (71)
The vessel containing the medicinal ingredients along with the mercury flows through the opening of the crucible;
likewise, by means of the three-fold apparatus for causing descent, [the substance] enters the two bodies.
The measure of this should be understood by the discerning from the mouth of the Guru;
because there is no fixed rule for the measurement of rasa, it cannot be described at all. (73)
Some [atoms] are equal in size to copper dust.
Now, another opinion is as follows:
"By means of peacock-neck [oxide] and mica, which have been reduced to a powder, one should perform the upward precipitation of the lord of mercury (rasendra) in a hand-drum (ḍamaruka). (74)
Mayūragrīva is tutthaka; tāpya is svarṇamākṣika; it is made into a "lost-and-pounded" (naṣṭapiṣṭa) preparation by means of the juice of the *kumārikā* plant—this is the remainder [of the sense].
Now, the process of downward precipitation (adhahpatana):
Having made the mercury into a "lost-paste" (naṣṭapiṣṭa) using triphalā, śigru, and śikhī, combined with salt and ammonium chloride (mūri), one should smear it inside an upper vessel. (75)
Having smeared the interior of the upper vessel, one should pour water into the lower vessel;
having applied a seal to the joint of the two, one should fill it with that [substance] until it reaches the eyebrows.
When a lid is placed on top, the mercury falls into the water;
this is called *adhaḥpātana* (downward precipitation) by the Siddhas and others in the process of distillation.

*Triphalā* has already been explained. Regarding the instruction "one should pour water into the lower vessel," it might be understood that water is placed inside the *sampuṭa* (the joined vessel), but that contradicts the traditional practice (*sampradāya*). Therefore, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: when the vessel is completely filled with water and buried in the ground, one should place the *sampuṭa* on top of it; subsequently, the joint between the *sampuṭa* and the lower vessel must be sealed.

When the *puṭa* is applied from above, the *puṭa* here—whether it be *kaeu-kuṭa*, according to the specific quantity of the liquid, or with twenty additional lotuses (*vanotpala*)—should be applied very slowly in a windless place; this is the tradition of the Gurus.

Now, another opinion is as follows: O Sūta, having ground abhraka with butter for a day with the juice of Jambha, [one should treat it] with Vānarī, Śigru, and Śikhin, combined with salt and Asurisa. (78)
"Having turned the mercury into a paste," and so forth, as previously described.
Now, the horizontal sublimation (*tiryakpātana*):
having poured the mercury into a jar, [one should place] another jar containing water [over it].
The wise one, having placed the two with their faces turned sideways, should block them together face-to-face.
In the same manner, having carefully placed [the vessel] upon the hearth, the physician should then kindle a fire beneath the liquid until it has flowed into the water. 80.
This is called *tiryakpātana* (horizontal falling), as taught by the Siddhas, Nāgārjuna, and others;
it occurs if lead and mercury are mixed together for the purpose of selling the elixir. (81)
From those two, an artificial defect may arise; its removal comes from the three *pātanas*.
Thus, having been well-purified with effort up to the stage of the *pātnī*, [he becomes a *sādhaka*]. 82.
He becomes completely liberated from all defects; there is no doubt about this. || 83 ||
At this point, some again express their reluctance, as follows:
"Having placed mercury in a cloth four times its weight and a śarāva-measure of sarasona, one should cook it for a day in a swinging-pot (dolikā) over a moderate fire. (84)
This sudation with a paste of *savyoṣa*, *triphalā*, *vahnikā*, and *nyāgrodha* in tepid water is prescribed for the purpose of eliminating the remaining morbid humors. (85)
Now, regarding awakening (bodhana):
when the *sūtra* is thus rendered useless, it attains a state of impotence (*ṣaṇḍhatva*).
For its liberation, awakening is performed; indeed, that is what is described here. (86)
Vāgbhaṭa also says: "By means of purifying *mardana* (rubbing) and *mūrchana* (fainting-inducing), the practitioner becomes one who brings about *mūraṇa* (swooning);
this should be understood as the excellence of power (*śaktyutkarṣa*) according to the method shown by the Guru. (87)
For example:
"Whether in a skull belonging to Viśvāmitra or even in a glass jar, having cast a lotus there, [one should wait] until it sinks therein. (88)
One should cook it on the ground for three days with a quantity of clarified butter equal to a *rāja* (one *karṣa*).
By this, this king of distillates (*srutarāja*) releases one from the state of impotence.

The *viśvāmitrakapāla* is a coconut vessel; some say it is "water produced at creation" (primordial water) or sea salt water, while others say it is urine, menstrual blood, and semen. However, the correct view is that "water produced at creation" refers to the urine of a healthy sixteen-year-old girl. A *rājahṛta* measures one and a quarter karas. Another opinion is easily understood [from the context]:
the neuter gender here is used for the sake of meter (*kūdurthana*). Thus ends the section on mercury.
But for one who has exerted great effort, it should be boiled in water containing rock salt on birch bark. (90)
1. "O gentle one! [The mercury] is pacified by the *pāta* method;
this is the opinion of another school—[namely], that the mercury placed inside a pot [should be treated] with salt and sour flour."
Then, having covered it and sprinkled a little water, one should seal it with a funnel.
Above, a light-sealed capsule should be applied; thus the mercury attains virility. || 92 ||
Another opinion holds:
indeed, semen that has been rendered useless reaches a state of impotence;
however, when it is treated with a decoction of many medicinal herbs, it becomes potent once again. (93)
Just as a potent [herb] is processed with *sarpākṣī*, *ciñcikā*, *vandhyā*, *bhṛṅga*, and *abdhi*,
that best of elixirs (*rasottama*) is produced, having cast off its neuter nature. (94)

*Sarpākṣī* is *nāgiṇī*; *ciñcā* is *amlikā*; *vandhyā* is *vājhakhakhasā*; *bhṛṅga* is *bhṛṅgarāja*; and *abda* refers to *mustā*, which should be understood as that known by the name *nāgara*. The juice of these [plants] is to be taken. Now, the regulation: with *sarpākṣī*, *ciñcikā*, *vanyā*, *bhṛṅga*, *abda*, *kanaka*, and water.
Exhausted by the day and drained of its impurities, it attains stability through the practice of restraint.
Another opinion:
having placed a large lump of red Saindhava salt from the northern region inside that [crucible], one should make nine apertures in it and pour the mercury (sūta) therein. || 96 ||
Then, having added chickpea alkaline water and lime juice on top, one should add a piece of rock salt. ||17||
Having prepared the ground and provided a hollow pit,
one should place a layer of eight finger-breadths of cow-dung cakes for a single day.
Having increased [the fire] and kindled it, one should wash that exterior with sour gruel (kāñjika).
This is called the purification known as *niyamana* by the wise. 99.
In the absence [of these], one should offer chickpea alkali (caṇakakṣāra) or natron (khārpa);
or else, salsoda (kharjikā) should certainly be given—thus said Bhāskara. 100.
Now, the process of inflaming (saṃdīpana): Take five parts of kāsīsa, rājikā, and black pepper, along with the seeds of viśigru, combined with ṭaṅkaṇa. (101)
One should boil it for three days in a swing-pot with sour gruel;
thus, the digestive fire of the king of mercury is properly kindled for the process of assimilation (jāraṇa). || 102 ||
Alternatively, one should cook it for three days in sour gruel (kāñjika) with the juices of the Citraka plant;
this produces the most excellent digestive stimulant (dīpana) for the king of mercury. 103.
Now, regarding the oil enema (anuvāsana):
one should heat the king of mercury (rasarāja) mixed with the juice of jambīra fruit and retain it for one day in a vessel made of clay or stone.
Thus ends the section on non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana).

The juice [of the drug] rubbed with the water of a thousand nimba fruits acquires a potency equal to fire; when combined with the three pungents (vyoṣa), cumin (rājī), salt, citraka, and asafoetida (rāmaṭhī), it remains effective for twenty days. (105)
Thus ends the section on non-unctuous enemas (anuvāsana) in the Rasacintāmaṇi.
Nityanātha, the author of the *Rasaratnākara*, states that when purified by these nine processes ending with *anuvāsana*, the mercury remains as one-eighth part after being strained:
"Purified by the nine operations beginning with *khedana* and so forth, it becomes free from its six sheaths (*kañcuka*).
When one-eighth part remains, it is then called 'purely strained' (*śuddhasruta*) by the wise."

The meaning is: "the examination for the purification of mercury. What kind of mercury, having been processed by the nine operations beginning with *khedana*, becomes free from its sheaths (*kañcuka*)? Regarding this, he states the observed proof (*dṛṣṭapratyaya*): (The examination for purifying it when freed from the sheaths). When one-eighth remains—that is, when seven parts related to the seven sheaths have departed and the eighth part of the mercury remains—then the mercury is pure, being liberated from the defects of the sheaths.

It is said: "The seven inner coverings (*kañcukas*) and the seven veils (*āvaraṇas*) were born from the curse of Śiva; by being liberated from them, one is called 'pure flow' (*śuddhasruti*) by the wise. Now, as for *jāraṇā* (digestion/assimilation): *Jāraṇā* indeed consists in the attainment of a previous state through the consumption of mercury, gold, and so forth, preceded by straining and precipitation, rather than by mere straining and precipitation alone. And its fruit was declared by Maheśvara himself: "When all sins have been destroyed, the digestion of mercury (*rasajāraṇā*) is attained.
Upon attaining that, the supreme knowledge characterized by liberation is truly attained."

Now, first, the digestion of sulfur (*gandhaka*).

Immediately after the propitiation of the deity prescribed in the *Tattva-tantra-nigada*, those of subtle intellect—observing the gradations of the purified mercury (*rasendra*) according to the analogy of fire produced by grass, cow-dung, or jewels through many extensive or concise purification rites (*śodhana-śrakiyā*)—should perform the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of mercury even with half a *pala*. Thus, taking some mercury according to the measure of two *vyāvahārika* *tolakas* as stated in the *Rasārṇava*: "The refinement of mercury must be performed even with half a *pala*," [they apply] therein the substance known as *gandhakanavanīta*.

Having purified [the mercury] according to the rule "one part [of mercury] and four parts [of the base]," and then having extracted it by the method of killing (māraṇa) and consumed it in the proper dose along with wholesome food (pathya), the mercury becomes a substance that produces the results described in such passages as "when the smell is equal, it destroys disease."

Now, if there is a desire for the qualities of an elixir (*rasāyana*), then after the digestion of sulfur (*gandhaka*), one should take mercury produced from the digestion of sulfur along with gold, mica, mineral essence (*sattva*), and so forth, according to one's means. Having killed it by the prescribed method of calcination (*māraṇa*) at the three junctions of the day (*saṃdhyā*), one should first "convert it into a field" (*kṣetrīkaraṇa*) and then consume it in the prescribed dose as part of a medicinal regimen (*pathyayoga*). This should be practiced for six months, a year, two years, or three years, up to the limit of a *maṇḍala*. Then one attains the aforementioned fruit. Or, if one possesses the necessary resources, it may be consumed for as long as one lives.

Alternatively, it should be consumed repeatedly according to one's capacity. However, if there is no desire for mere medicinal treatment, then after purifying the mercury through the processing stages beginning with *khedana* (sweating) and ending with *dīpana* (stimulation), and having sublimated it with sulphur (*gandhaka*) according to the prescribed method, it should be consumed in the proper dose as part of a medicinal regimen until health is restored.

Now, regarding the application of mercury (rasa) in preparations such as decoctions, electuaries, pills, powders, and the like, the secret instruction of the masters is as follows: once the formulation has been prepared according to the prescribed words, the mercury should be employed only after it has undergone purification (*saṃśuddha*), been processed with sulfur (*mūrchita*), or has been digested within gold and other metals (*jīrṇa*), or is "dead" (*mṛta*) or "immortalized" (*amṛta*). Even if purified, mercury that lacks the digestion by sulfur must not be used in formulations, because its capacity to act as a catalyst (*gandhatva-śakti*) has not arisen. Furthermore, even if digested in gold and other metals, mercury that has not been purified must never be used anywhere, as it produces defects. In this same manner, all secondary minerals (*uparasa*), primary metals (*dhātu*), minor metals (*upadhātu*), gems (*ratna*), minor gems (*uparatna*), poisons (*viṣa*), and counter-poisons (*upaviṣa*), and so forth, [must be treated accordingly].

Being pure, whether dead or immortal, they should be applied according to the literal statement; those who are impure should not be, such is the general direction. In this world, indeed, since suffering is the object of unconditioned aversion for a person, its absence must be sought to be achieved; likewise, happiness, being the locus of unconditioned love, is to be pursued. These two constitute the dual ends of human life (*puruṣārtha*).

In this regard, objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and women—though they are the causes of pleasure—are to be abandoned because they are invariably accompanied by suffering; because they are beset by a succession of misfortunes; because they appear to fools like a mirage in the sky; because they are inconclusive (anaikāntika); because their opposites are not seen simultaneously; and because they are never entirely separated from suffering.

Furthermore, these means—namely Jñānayoga (the yoga of knowledge), Prāṇayoga (the yoga of vital breath), and Rasayoga (the yoga of alchemy)—are indeed equally effective in their ultimate and final goal, just like Hari, Hara, and Brahmā. Now, to address the question of how they are equal, we cite the words of Vasiṣṭha in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Vṛhad-Vāsiṣṭha*: "No single method is impossible for anyone to achieve certainty through knowledge. Therefore, the supreme Lord Śiva spoke of two ways:
either by the restraint of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) or by the removal of latent mental impressions (*vāsanās*). (125)

therefore, their equality is beyond reproach. In this regard, since even those whose passions (*kleśa*) are merely ripened can somehow achieve success through the first two [methods], whereas through the last one even those who are greedy for worldly enjoyment possess the qualification [for practice], to whom would it not appear that this [third method] is superior to the other two? Furthermore, as this [method] is the very essence of the Blessed One, how many modulations (*mūrcchanā*) of its qualities can there be—qualities which cause the servants [of this method] to become identical with all the constituent elements (*dhātu*) of the Blessed Lady, the Queen of Mercury (*rasarāja*), the ocean of virtues? These shall be illustrated here in passing.
Now, *mūrcchanā* is that which invariably destroys disease; its varieties are of many kinds. Among them:

1. It means like a hollow in the sky, or like a city of the Gandharvas. It is called "kha" because it appears like the interior of a sheath (*kośāṇḍa*); it is called "ka" because it appears like the inner chamber of musk (*keśarakastūrikākośa*). 2. The sense is that it is the cause of bliss. Intoxication (*mūrcchanā*) is of two kinds, distinguished by being odorless (*nirgandha*) or having fragrance (*sagandha*). Odorless intoxication is uniform in nature, produced by poisons and medicinal herbs, and is approved by the supreme yogis. That which has fragrance, however, is of three types: external, internal, and smoke-like.

The threefold [process] is further divided into five types according to the distinctions of *gandhapiṣṭi*, *gandhabaddha*, *gandhajīrṇa*, *sagandhakañjalī*, and *dhātupiṣṭi*. And *dhātupiṣṭi* is fivefold according to the distinctions of gold, silver, copper, lead, and iron. Furthermore, *mūrchana* and *jāraṇā* are generally synonymous; that [process] is twofold by means of internal smoke and fire, distinguished as *iṣṭikā*, *kācakūpī*, *kācasapuṭa*, and *suvarṇayantra*.

In this regard, the battle-born (*jāraṇā*) produced from the six qualities is declared to be most excellent; however, that must be performed upon the King of Mercury (*rasarāja*) which has been bound by the purificatory processes (*saṃskāra*) such as sweating (*khedana*) and rubbing (*mardana*). Binding (*bandhana*), moreover, consists in being rendered solid (*mūrtibaddhatva*) through fire despite possessing its natural fluidity; that occurs by means of the purificatory processes ending with *niyama*. Now, for one who is unable to perform the purificatory processes such as sweating and so forth, there are also taught easy methods for the purification of mercury.

Regarding mercury (*pārada*), they state its examination as follows: "That which is deep blue within and brilliant without, with a luster like the midday sun, is to be employed; likewise, that which is smoky or pale white is to be employed; but that which is variegated is not to be employed for the accomplishment of alchemical works.

Thus [it is said]. Now, regarding the sublimation (*jāraṇa*) of sulphur by means of the tortoise-vessel (*kacchapayantra*), Śārṅgadhara says:
"One should place water in an earthen pit and a small cup (*śarāvaka*) in its center."
In the center, there is the emergence of the *meṣa* [Aries] sign, resembling the covering of a great vessel. (582) [Note:
'samaguṇe' is the reading in manuscript *kha*.]
Having placed it within the middle of the girdle, one should pour mercury into it with powder;
over the mercury, one should add an equal portion of sulphur powder.
Having placed a shallow bowl on top, one should cause the ash-seal (bhasmamudrā) to be applied;
then, one should place a cover over it using four lumps of cow dung. || 184 ||
In this manner, the wise one should repeatedly digest the fragrance six times over.
When the fragrance is digested, it becomes liquefied, possessing a sharp fire and performing all functions. Thus [it is said].
In the *Rasaratnākara*:
Having placed a *pakvamūṣā* on a bed of cow-dung, one should pour the oil extracted from bitter *tuṃbī* into its center and then drop the mercury therein. (186)
The juice of *kākamācī* should be given repeatedly in an amount equal to the oil;
then, having added sulphur the size of a grain of rice, one should seal it. (187)
On a flat surface, one should place a full earthen vessel or a skull-cup;
having ascertained that its body has become cool, one should repeatedly add and digest old oil, sulphur, and the juice of *kākamācī*. (188)
Having seen the thick [substance] produced from cow-products and having heated it upwards, one should digest it six times with sulfur; thus the mouth of the crucible becomes as if melted. || 189 ||
Thus ends the section on *ajāraṇa*.

Now, regarding *anlaya*: having placed the mercury according to the prescribed measure along with sand and *akhbayaca* into a small earthen vessel, one should pour in the liquid mercury that remains after the oil has been extracted; this should be done again after observing that the digestion (*mārdhaka*) is complete. 190.
One should add a very small amount of sulphur possessing eight qualities; the mercury, having digested the offering (bali), becomes exceedingly powerful.
When employed in all mercurial preparations, this [sulphur] undoubtedly destroys disease with speed. 191.
Thus ends the sublimation of sulfur.
This reading is not found in manuscript Kha.
Now, the digestion of gold (*svarṇajāraṇa*).
As it has been said:
First, one should perform the digestion of sulphur; then the digestion of gold;
then the digestion of the essence of mercury (jaladhara-sattva); and thereafter, the digestion of all the metals.
Now, the description of the *viḍa* (digestive flux) useful for that [process]: substances that produce an intense hunger for swallowing gold and other metals are called *viḍas*. For example:
having pierced it with eight fingers' breadth of clay from a *vajrakaṇṭaka* or *vajrāgra*, and having smeared it with cow-dung, it is roasted in a mild fire and dried there. (193)
Thrown into the hollow of the Vajra for three days, the mercury becomes hungry;
it then devours scents, gold, and so forth, as well as Vajrasattva and the others, in an instant. 194.

Another method is as follows: the mercury, which has been processed with the six qualities mentioned in the chapter on *mūrchana* (coagulation), is placed in a mortar along with digested (*jīrṇa*) flour-paste; then, being intensely hungry, it quickly swallows thick gold, diamond, and the essence of iron. Others practice by performing both of these methods. Now, other [methods] are said:
"With *tuṭṭhaka*, borax, and *sajai*, and salt, one should soak copper for three days in sour gruel (*kāñjika*).
By means of that, mercury (*gandha*) and the others swallow [the metal] in an instant. (195)
When cast into the bile of a vulture, the mercury becomes eager for union;
it swallows all metals, all living beings, and even diamond.
Now, another method:
one should soak conch-shell powder in the juice of ripe jambīra for one day, along with dhūmasāra, for one day. (197)
Sauvarcala salt should be soaked in goat's urine for four watches (yāmas), and kaṇṭakārī should be boiled for one day in human urine. (198)
One should boil date-palm alkali, *tuṇṭuka*, *uḍīcya*, *kāsīsa*,
and *śilājatu* separately with the juice of *jambīra* for four watches (yāmas) each.
One should soak rock salt (*saindhava*) and borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*) for one day in the juices of *jayapāla* seeds and radishes (*mūlaka*), and for one day in the water of *guñjā* and *śiśu* roots. (200)
Having thoroughly ground all of this with the juice of *jambīra* fruits, one should carefully preserve that *bhola*; this is the *viḍa* known as *vaḍavānala*. (201)
The mercury, processed with this and placed in that mortar,
instantly devours all metallic essences, such as iron and the rest.
Thus is the submarine fire described.

One should take a liquid alkaline solution strained through cloth, prepared from radish and fresh ginger boiled in cow’s urine; with this, one should saturate sulphur one hundred times in a hot, dry place. This is *viḍa* salt for the digestion of gold. (203)
Thus ends the *biḍa* as described in the *Siddhalakṣmīśvaratantra*.
In this manner, the other *biḍas* should also be followed there from the intermediate [text]; such is the explanation of the *biḍas*.
One should take hemp leaves (*hempatra*) sixty parts and peacock feathers (*māyūra*) one part;

having placed them in a heated mortar (*taptakhalva*) with a liquid, one should grind them. This procedure—rubbing for two days with the juice of *jambīra* (citron)—is to be applied at every morsel (*grāsa*). || 204 ||
Having bound it with common salt in a vessel of *kāñjika* juice, one should gently rub it on birch bark;
after three days, one should extract the mercury from the vessel once the gold has been digested. (205)
If it has been raised too much, it should be scorched again until it reaches equilibrium;
one should cause the eight [parts] to dissolve in the sequence of thirty-two, sixteen, and eight.
And for beings such as those made of silver and so forth, this same procedure is prescribed;
in the absence of a hearth, salt, and fragrance, [the rite is performed] by means of fire and bile.
Thus ends the procedure for the sublimation (*jāraṇa*) of all substances, such as silver and the like, by means of *khaṇa*.
Now, the characteristics of *taptakhala*:
having buried goat dung and salt in the ground, one should cast [the substance] into it.
Situated above that is the mortar; it is that very mortar. 208.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the heated mortar.
Now, according to the Siddhamata, the digestion of gold by means of a swinging crucible (*dolāyantra*) is as follows:
One should thoroughly rub [the gold] with five or six parts of *dhruvakṣāra* along with a "swallow" (*sagrāsa*).
That [mixture] should then be combined with mercury (*mūta*) in a sixteenfold proportion, or with sulfur (*gandha*) in an eightfold proportion. (209)
Then, having macerated it in the juice of *jambīra* or in *kāñjika*, a *dolāpāka* (swing-cooking) should be performed; this is known as the *dolāyantra* (swinging apparatus).
The sense is that the process of heating in a swing (dolāpāka) should be performed for three days or until the substance is digested.
This concludes the section on heating in a swing.
Now, another method according to the Siddhamata for the extraction of gold by means of the tortoise apparatus (kacchapayantra), as follows:
A baked crucible (pakamūṣā) is one that has been constantly held over a vessel of water so that it remains positioned within the opening of a shallow bowl;
its interior is covered with mercury and thirty-two parts of bīḍa salt. || 211 ||
Then, having enclosed it in an iron vessel and sealed it with a firm seal,
one should pour in sand measuring eight finger-breadths in height.
When that mercury is blown upon with the *iṭhā* [wind] and established within its essence,
it certainly consumes gold smeared with peacock-feather ash.
Thus ends the description of the tortoise machine.
And it is said:
Having placed a small bowl over the mouth of a vessel filled with water that has a hole,
one should apply a baked crucible over the hole so that there is no separation from the water.
Its mouth, covered with iron, should be filled with mercury enclosed by bitumen.
Having placed sand on top and having applied the seal, it is blown and blown very gradually;
as if swallowing each time it is blown, it attains subtlety within the sound.
Those of small intellect seek [mercury] that is slightly heated with bile and slowly dried to a balanced state, for the sake of the body or for the purpose of alchemy. (216)
Thus also ends the "Tortoise-Skin" chapter.
1. "Kāñcanakaraṇa" Kha! Now, according to another opinion:
[one should perform the rite] in a vessel made of iron, containing water from a pit, along with *viḍa* salt, a morsel of food, and *īśvaraja* [mud].
Having covered it with a flattened iron vessel and sealed it with wax, one should apply heat.
By this much alone, the purpose of the elixir (*rasāyana*) is fulfilled; however, the [theoretical] discourse is not the primary concern.
Thus ends the section on the digestion of gold (*hemajāraṇā*).

Now, regarding digestion (*jāraṇā*) by means of the predominance of both [the seed and the metal] together, therein occurs the digestion of the essence (*sattva*) of the ore (*ghana*). As it has been said: "Those wretched ones who have accomplished their purpose by digesting seeds devoid of ore, yet remain satisfied with obtaining a mere cowrie shell upon reaching the ocean. (218)
Except for the single essence of the cloud (the mercury), no other is capable of cutting through the wings of the alchemical elixir;
therefore, with its movement obstructed by that, it is restrained and easily bound.
One should always discard red and yellow [pigments] for the sake of gold, black [pigments] for those with golden bodies, and white [pigments] for the work of silver, as well as glass and dross.

Having added [the ingredients] bit by bit, the mercury (rasendra) along with mica-essence, gold, and so forth, is rubbed in a warm mortar; it dissolves in earth, water, and the acids of *aveta*, *jambīra*, and *bījapūra*.
(221) "Earth and bird" refers to *kāsīsa* (green vitriol). In the absence of acid, previously prepared sour gruel (*kāñjika*) should also be understood as acceptable. And another [author] says:

He who does not know first the digestion of mica, then the rapid digestion within the womb, and finally the digestion of gold, is no speaker at all; he merely acts out of vanity after having looked [into the texts]. 222.
Thus ends the digestion of the essence of mica.
Now, regarding the extraction of the embryo (*garbhadrutī*):

When combined with the essence of *tāpya* (cinnabar) equal in measure to the essence of *vyoma* (mica), the mercury, having moved completely, O Goddess, becomes the "embryo-extractor" (*garbhadrāvī*). || 223 ||

In this manner, *hematārābhra* and other such substances were formulated by Khukharipu; they should be employed after observing the specific purpose [of the process]. Without the *garbhaduti*, there can be no *jāraṇā* (digestion).

Therefore, he states its definition: *Garbhaduti* is the liquefaction of those [substances] that have been swallowed by the mercury (*rasa*), even in the absence of fire. The purification (*saṃskāra*) of the *bījas* (seeds) must be performed through their union with *tāpyasattva*.
By means of the sour group [of substances], they flow into the womb as the king of essences (rasarāja). || 224 ||
A seed destroyed by a stone, or burnt by fire, or carried away by the Sindhu river,
or killed by both of these, perishes in an instant at the time of sowing.
Now, the process of swinging (dolājāraṇa):

Having smeared [the vessel] with a paste of the six salts, alkali, cow’s urine, and milk-hedge plant (juhī) juice, and having bound it on the outside with a cloth, one should place it inside a birch-bark leaf. 226.
The physician should cause [the mercury] to sweat for three days in alkali, sour gruel, and urine;
by this sequence, having caused it to digest four morsels in a swinging vessel (dolāyantra), he should then digest the mercury in fire using the kacchapayantra method. (227)
Thus ends the descent into the womb. Now, the measure of the movement of the morsel (grāsa):
the first is sixty-four parts, the second is thirty-two parts, the third consists of sixteen parts, and the fourth is eight parts. (228)
O Goddess of the Gods, from the sixty-fourth morsel, the mercury becomes a bearer of the staff;
however, in the second stage of swallowing, it is like a leech.
With the third morsel, he becomes like crow-dung;
with the fourth morsel, he becomes like whey. || 230 ||

Other matters have not been written here because they are difficult to understand; however, the venerable Govinda Pāda writes that [the mercury] is indeed digested by a sixteenth part (kalāṃśa). For example:
"Having first caused the impurity (enas) to be consumed by exactly five parts, one who is skilled in the process of separation then digests the three parts by a sixteenth part. (231)

1. "Some such [person] first" is the reading in the *Rasahṛdaya*. 2. "By the addition of sourness to the king of juices. 3. "He becomes a bearer of the staff" means that his clothing and food do not leak away; according to that view, there are five morsels consisting of sixty-four, forty-four, thirty, twenty-eight, sixteen, and five [units]. Now, the coloring process (*rañjana*).
In the act of piercing, such an application is not observed.
Pure, stainless copper, when treated with cinnabar, becomes threefold [in weight] once digested, and its liquid assumes the appearance of lac juice.
One should digest the nāga killed by gandhaka within the interior of a lotus;
when three times this amount has been digested, the mercury becomes the color of lac. (233)

Within the interior of the *kamala* (lotus), this [seed] is not for the purpose of an elixir (*rasāyana*) because of its connection with the serpent (*nāga*). Just as it is said, once the seed has been processed three times over copper (*tāmra*), that seed, having become fully digested (*samajīrṇa*), dyes [the metal] by means of that very [process].

Or, gold is brought forth (*nivyūḍha*) from that seed by means of *kunaṭī* (realgar) acting upon lead, or by the sun acting upon mercury, or by iron acting upon sulphur, or by tin acting upon cinnabar. || 234 ||
Even the *Kevalārka* array, when formed by a powerful king.
Kunaṭī is realgar; karināga is lead; ravi is copper; and asileḍhva is iron.
Now, regarding the seed of silver (tārabīja):
one should prepare a fine powder of equal parts of kuṭila (tin), vimalā (antimony), and tīkṣṇa (steel).
One should slowly recite the *tāra* mantra ten times, enfolded five times;
thus the auspicious *tāra* seed-syllable becomes tenfold in power. (235)
Kuṭila is vaṅga (tin), vimalā is kākhamākṣika (a type of pyrite), and tīkṣṇa is iron.
Having made the essence extracted from tāla equal to the vaṅga, one should heat it;
then one should process that powder into silver until it possesses sixteen times the quality.
This is the most excellent seed of faith, the bond of the flow;
through digestion and transmutation, it pierces by a thousandth part.

1. [The term] ‘rañjanavedhana’ is found in manuscript Ka. 2. [The reading] ‘triguṇatāmrajāraṇādanu tadbhaya’ is found in manuscript Kha. 3. [The reading] ‘khatantreṇaiva’ is found in manuscript Kha. [From the Āyurvedaprakāśa: 238. One should cause tin-mercury (vaṅgābhra) to permeate silver; it indeed possesses twelve qualities. When this equal amount of seed has been digested, the mercury becomes a hundred-fold penetrator (śatavedhī). 239. Now, regarding the gold-seed: one should cause lead-mercury (nāgābhra) to permeate gold, and it likewise possesses twelve qualities. This is the most excellent seed for the binding of mercury.

Copper or silver killed with honey should be repeatedly colored; one should then carry that lead through the seed [bīja] sixteen times. This seed is proclaimed to be the most excellent and superior, known as the lead-seed (nāgabīja); by merely being processed an equal amount, it pierces [the metal] even in a thousandth part. Now, for the purpose of coloring and transmuting (sāraṇa), the oil [is prepared from]: mañjiṣṭhā, kiṃśuka, khadira, red sandalwood, karavīra, devadāru, sarala, and the two types of turmeric.

Having ground other red flowers with lac juice, one should cook oil with it and use that for the collyrium of the eyes and so forth. O Goddess of the Gods, one should prepare [the paste] with double the amount of red flowers and the group of red and yellow [pigments], four times as much milk, and one part oil (244). [The oil should be derived] from *jyotiṣmatī*, *karañja*, *akṣa*, and bitter *tumbī*; [it should be processed] separately with the juices of *pāṭalā*, *kākatuṇḍī*, *ambu*, *hārāṣṭrī*, and [the meat of] frogs, boars, rams, snakes, mongooses, tortoises, and leeches.

Combined with an equal portion of fat (*vasā*) and sixteen parts of well-ground *bhūlatā*, *amalākṣīka*, the two *dvandvamelāpaka* medicinal herbs, and processed by heating and straining, it is called *sāraṇātaila*. Herein, *gandharvataila* is also mentioned according to the *Rasahṛdaya-kharasa*. Now, the *dvandvamelāpaka* medicinal herbs: "wool (*ūrṇā*), *ṭaṅkaṇa*, mountain-resin (*girijatu*), buffalo-ear-dirt, eye-dirt, *śakragopa*, and *karka*"—these are the *dvandvamelāpaka* medicinal herbs. (From the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter 34).

Now, another method: one should add four times the amount of liquid to oil extracted from *kaṅguṇī* seeds along with white flowers produced from various trees according to their availability (verse 248). One should cook it until only the oil remains, and then pour into that oil the molten seed of silver (*tāra*) twenty-one times; thus, the coloring of the king of liquids (*rasarāja*) becomes perfectly dyed (verse 249). Furthermore, there is excessive strength in mercury (*kuṭila*), color in sulfur (*tīkṣṇa*), and oiliness in mica (*pannaga*).

But they praise the powers of mercury (rāma) when it is bound by the strength of love for the lotus-dweller (kamalānilaya). || 250 || Strength resides in the essence of mica (abhraka); digestion (jāraṇa) and coloring (rāga) are established in the sharp metal (tīkṣṇa). Binding (bandha), however, occurs in the common metal (sāraloha); then, transmutation (krāmaṇa) takes place in lead and tin. || 251 || The mercury transmutates by means of the sharp metal; by the sharp metal, the morsel (grāsa) is digested. The source of gold is the sharp metal; it acquires colorings through the sharp metal. || 252 || And that [sharp metal] is killed by cinnabar (darada), or having been killed by honey (mākṣika) together with copper (ravi).

Even that which has been perfumed by the *vāsana* should be processed like a solid mass and then subjected to *jāraṇā*. (253) Like a solid cloud or a dense mass, when these metals—along with *mākṣika*—are combined and quickly processed within the crucible (*garbha*) through the application of *viḍa*, the King of Mercury attains *bandha*. (254) When it is "seedless" (*nirbīja*), fully digested (*samajīrṇa*), and reduced by one-quarter, [the result is] sixteen parts gold; by half, one-quarter gold; and by one-eighth, equal gold. (255)

The fitness for *sāraṇā* (transmutation) and the capacity for piercing [the metal] a hundred times or more belong to that which is fully digested (*jīrṇa*). For that which is less than fully digested, there is only the authority for coating the leaf (*patralepa*). As it is said in the *Rasahṛdaya*: 1. “The experts in metals say... 2. “Then the *sāraṇā* with lead and tin... 3. “Slain by *mākṣika* (pyrite)... 4. “In the case of the digested... the digested... 5. “When seedless and fully digested, by a single quarter, namely a sixteenth part.”

"By half [of the mercury] there is union with the feet, and by one foot it is equal to gold"—this is the reading in the *Rasahṛdaya*. [From the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*: The leaf, having its surface polished and its veins and other parts cleansed, is made perfectly pure. Then, having smeared it with mercury, it is coated with the *krāmaṇa* (transmuting) agent and rested within crucibles (*puṭa*). The crucible is generally placed beneath a *cūlikā* (mound). Having mixed that leaf with half of the finest gold, it is subjected to the *puṭa* process. Then, this *varṇapuṭa* (coloring crucible) should be applied using clay colored with earth, bird-bile, and vermilion.

257 || "By half" is an elliptical expression. *Kṣitikhaga* is *kāsīsa* (green vitriol). Furthermore— With cords made of *bhela*, *kvaṅga*, and *ibha*, and with the essence of *ruta* and *bhaya*, iron and copper are bound by mercury and *vetaṇa* according to the method bestowed by the venerable Guru. 258 || The four minerals, *gandha* and *īśa*, made into gold within a glass flask, constitute a formulation for the sake of nectar that is superior even to the application of chalk. 259 || Equal parts of *maṇḍūka*, mercury, *śilā*, and *balaya*, well-ground together with *kṣiti*, *vela*, *śaya*, *marta*, and *jihva*...

In this matter, by means of that which has been explained by the teachers, [the results] fall here in very few days; indeed, one does not experience astonishment. Having caused iron, sulphur, and borax to revolve, one should cause a frog mixed with that to revolve as well. Having prepared cinnabar (tāla) between the fourth and the fifth [elements], that is within the "Form-Mine" (rūpakhānta) according to the seeds taught by the Siddhas. In the *Siddhamata*, there are two seeds: *lohamekī* and *tārabe-kī*.

The sprinkling of molten mercury upon tin and copper produces fragments of vermilion and pieces of mica. 1. *Bheka* means mica (*abhraka*); *ibha* means elephant (*nāga*). 2. *Sāraloha* refers to gold and silver. 3. *Rasavaṭa* means mercury-elephant (*rasamātaṅga*). 4. *Maṇḍūka* means mica (*abhraka*). 5. "With the tongue of the machine"—*kṣiti* means green vitriol (*kāsīsa*), *bileśaya* means snake (*nāga*), and *mantrajihva* means fire; the meaning is gold. 6. By the best of machines, namely the *ambhūdhara* (earth-bearing) machine.

Having stirred together sulphur and borax with wine, one should melt iron and mica (*abhra*) in that mixture over the fire. One should liquefy it; this is the perfected seed (*siddhabīja*) called "Iron-Mica" (*lohabheki*). Then, having applied *tāla* (mica/minium) within the interior of tin (*vaṅga*)—meaning having extracted the tin by means of *tāla*—one should place that tin inside silver and melt that silver in the aforementioned perfected seed. This, however, is the perfected seed called "Silver-Mica" (*tārabheki*).

8. *Dardura* (frog), *abhra* (mica), the two base metals (*pūtiloha*)—lead (*nāga*) and tin (*vaṅga*)—when these are combined and melted, and if a drop is placed upon a piece of *hiṅgula* (cinnabar), it causes the cutting off of its wings; that is to say, an ash of two fingers' breadth is produced. [Āyurvedīyagranthamālā, Vol. 36, Chapter on *Śaśiheli*. "By this, the wealth of those whose intellects are unfailing is certainly licked by the moon. Thus ends the *khoṭa* (pill) according to the *Siddhamata*. Here, words such as *bheka* (frog) and others denote metallic ores; there is no need for further revelation of the secret.

A paste made from a pair of *gandha-taila* and iron will proceed toward putrid water; likewise, a paste prepared with oil, frogs, and *bali* [offerings], through ablutions with monkey-fuel (*plavaga-pūlya*). (263) Since mercury (*darada*) is also taken as a paste, it is connected to the previous operation. Thus, in the Siddhamata, there is the *khoṭa* [solidified product]. Eight finger-breadths below the hearth, the sands placed within the crucible are perfected; through heating with mercury, sulphur, and mica, they are transformed by the fire. (264)

Another *khoṭa*: Mercury is bound by a crooked line of charcoal from *sālera*, *kuṭilārka*, *sthara*, *rambhā*, and *pāmārga*, as if by a *hrutī* [impurity], using a fragment of crooked iron. (265) Another *khoṭa*: Mercury is bound by a circular wheel of iron, as if by a *hrarūtī* [impurity], using the alkaline ash of *bheka*, *bhāskara*, *gandhāśmā*, and tin (*vaṅga*). (266) Thus end the processes of coloring (*rañjana*) and piercing (*vedhana*). Now, the external fluxes (*bāhyadrutayaḥ*).

These, when combined as a mere *āroṭaka* (elixir), bring about immortality; its fruit is a lifespan measured by a kalpa, or else, when digested according to the previously mentioned sequence of consumption, it yields the aforementioned results. [The terms are: *śaśi* is silver, *tāra* is mercury, *heliraka* is copper, and *hiraṇya* is gold; mice made of these [metals] bestow constant fortune (*dhruva-lakṣmī*), meaning that [fortune] arises from sprinkling [the elixir] upon them.

2. *Gandhatailayugalā* means accompanied by fragrant oil; *piṣṭhī* is the name for *darada* (cinnabar). It will come under the control of putrid water—that is, it will come under the control of the liquid (*vāri*) of those two, lead and tin (*nāgavaṅgau*), which are putrid metals; the meaning is that it will not fly upward in the fire. 3. *Vaśameti ca* (it comes under control), as found in manuscript *kha*.

4. A pill (*piṭī*) consisting of mercury and sulfur (*rasagandhakayoḥ*) mixed with oil, frogs, and sacrificial offerings (*tailabhekabalibhiḥ*), when consecrated (*abhiṣeka*) by means of monkey-pus (*plavagapūya*), ash (*kṣvaga*), mica (*abhraka*), and the two base metals (*pūtilohau*), namely lead (*nāga*) and tin (*vaṅga*), results in the restraint (*saṃyama*) of those [metals] once they have been melted together. (Note: *mātchra* is a variant reading; this is from the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*, verse 37. There are thirty-seven [such] applications.

And it is said: when [the mercury] has been digested once, it is a "piercer of a hundred" (śatavedhī); when digested twice as much, it is a "piercer of a thousand" (sahasravedhī); in this manner, one should proceed with the piercings of a hundred thousand, ten thousand, and ten million. However, when digested sixty-four times, it penetrates by the mere touch of its fumes, or even by its sound. Now, the process of *sāraṇā* (coagulation) is described: A blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) should be made, resembling the shape of a cow's teat; that same crucible, provided with a small opening and shallow in depth, is suitable for *sāraṇā*. (267)

In this very crucible, one should fill it with oil that is free from dregs and pure; while that oil is intensely heated, at the very moment of throwing the molten seed into it, the excellent flux (srutavara) must be well-swirled around. Immediately thereafter, the mouth of the crucible must be covered by tying a knot in a piece of cloth soaked in that oil. When combined with red and white seeds through this process of *sāraṇā* (merging), it is to be known as *saṃsārita* (well-merged) and properly restrained (*saṃyamita*). However, *pratisārita* (re-merged) occurs with double the amount of seed, and *anusārita* (after-merged) is likewise.

The mercury that has digested old mica (*jīrṇābhraka*), whose odor is completely vanished, and which has been reduced to ash after digesting all the foremost metals, is called *nirjīva*; it destroys all diseases with great force when combined with the ashes of lead. Furthermore, mercury that has digested gold and has been made into a paste through the application of sulfur, then successively encapsulated by equal parts of sulfur, is named *nirbīja* and destroys every ailment. That mercury which has been thoroughly processed (*parijārita*) with the seeds (*bīja*) of mica-essence, gold, copper, silver, and magnetite, is likewise a destroyer of all diseases.

Then, extracted by means of the sixfold fragrance (*ṣaḍguṇagandhaka*) and bound with the seed-syllables (*saṃvījabaddha*), the mercury (*sūta*) becomes possessed of vast power. Another [type] is extracted from *vajra* and other substances; when equalized, it is bound with chains (*śṛṅkhalābaddha*). This mercury, which effects the transformation of the body and metals, pervades all things with its diverse nature through its speed—thus does Śaṅkara know. Even when processed with external fluxes (*bāhyadruti*), whether it has attained fixation (*bandha*) or exists in the form of ash, that mercury, when measured at one-quarter of a *rājikā* seed, destroys diseases that are difficult to cure; it is known by the name *drutibaddha*.

The child (Bāla) mercury, born of Śiva, when digested with an equal amount of mica and properly consumed while engaged in yoga, acts as a Rasāyana that swiftly removes future diseases and destroys ailments along with their complications and fatal signs. That which is born of Hara (Harodbhava), when digested with double the amount of mica, is called the youth (Kumāra); it requires a limited amount of rice and, within twenty-one nights, truly destroys the multitude of sinful diseases and serves as a Rasāyana. That which consumes four times the amount of mica is known as the adolescent (Taruna); it is the foremost among Rasāyanas.

After seven nights, that mercury (rasa), having digested its entire impurity, becomes an elixir (rasāyana) that bestows vigor and strength. That mercury which has digested abhraka six times over and has attained friendship with fire is known as "the aged" (vṛddha); it should be employed in both the body and in metallurgy—who, other than Śiva, can describe its qualities? Indeed, this mercury, once born, is not diminished by fire.

When applied against all diseases, it bestows incomparable results. Some [mercury] is used in conjunction with *rasabhasma* (mercurial ash), while some *mūrchita* is for the sake of the body. (349) Now, the process of reducing mercury to ash (*rasabhasmīkaraṇa*).

In that regard, the "elephant-ash" known as *rasasindūra* is prepared as follows: five *palas* of mercury, an equal portion of purified sulfur free from defects, one *ṭaṅka* of sulphur, and one *karṣa* of *tuvarī*, are thoroughly rubbed together. (Āyurvedīya Granthamālā, 46).

Now, in the Rasavāgbhaṭa: Mercury that has been processed (*saṃdhita*) and placed within a horn, a tooth, a bamboo tube, or similar vessel—having worshipped the gods, cows, and Brahmins according to one’s capacity (474)—one should drink it after it has been strained through a leaf-cup as an after-drink (*anupāna*). It may be combined with ghee, rock salt (*saindhava*), coriander (*dhānyāka*), cumin (*jīraka*), and fresh ginger (*ārdraka*). [One may also consume] *taṇḍulīyaka*, coriander, *paṭola*, *alābu*, and so forth. Cumin seeds (*kustumbarī*), black pepper (*marīca*), and rock salt should be taken in equal parts (475–476).

For the sake of flavor, one who seeks the best taste should consume food prepared with wheat, aged *śāli* rice, cow's milk, ghee, and curd. (477) A small amount of green gram soup is proclaimed as the group of wholesome foods. One should avoid the *bṛhatī*, *bilva*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, the tips of *vetra* canes, and *kāravellaka*. (478) One should also avoid black gram, peacock, flat beans, horse gram, mustard, and sesame; as well as meat from birds caught in snares, red cocks, and fermented liquors (*surā-āsava*). (479) One should eat meat from marshy animals and sour gruel on plantain leaves.

One should avoid mercury that is stale, heavy, constipating, sharp, or hot; the wise man should avoid what is forbidden and consume it with various tastes and juices. (480) So that the mercury does not leak out and the digestive fire is not destroyed. (481) Now, regarding the remedy for the poison if mercury has been consumed by mistake without being purified, he says: "If, somehow through ignorance, mercury tainted by lead or other impurities has been eaten, the wise man should drink the root of *Kāravechu* to cause its excretion. (482)

Now, the best of physicians should recognize great diseases when there is indigestion of *rasa* (chyle). In cases of aggravation of *vāyu*, one should perform anointing with oils such as *nārāyaṇa* and others. (This portion of the text is not found in the Kha and Ga manuscripts. [Āyurvedīya Granthamālā] In cases of aversion to food, one should sprinkle cold water on the head; for thirst, coconut water or green gram soup mixed with sugar is recommended.

In the event of vomiting, one should take rice with curd, black cumin, and rock salt; or the juice of *sindhuvāra*, *karkoṭī*, cow’s urine, and *kāravellī* boiled together. (486) One should drink any one of these as a digestive tonic (*rasāyana*) for indigestion: *śarapuṅkhā*, *suradālī*, seeds of *paṭola*, and *kākamācī*. (487) Hārīta said: Among all grains and the like, barley, wheat, and *ṣaṣṭika* rice are preferred; however, all legumes are not desired, except for mung beans and *āḍhakī*. (488)

Clarified butter is the best among syrups, and among sweets, that which is produced from sugarcane is superior; indeed, refined sugar is excellent, provided it is not mixed with alkaline substances. Asafoetida is the best among all fragrant aromatics, rock salt among salts from the Indus region, and soups made with turmeric and ginger are supreme among root vegetables. (489) However, unwholesome leaf-vegetables and all types of split pulses do not cause harm when prepared according to the prescribed method. (490)

Food that is infested with hair or other impurities, over-cooked or under-cooked, excessively abundant, mixed with many vegetables and inferior grains, burnt by excessive heat, kept overnight, or overly salty—such food should be avoided by those who practice *rasāyana*. Buttermilk is beneficial, as is curd that has been processed with fats; all products derived from cow’s milk are wholesome when consumed. However, one must exclude oil, water, wine, and sour gruel (*surāranāla*). Drinking water during *rasāyana* is not beneficial. As for oils, those produced from *citrā*, from mountain minerals (*girijā*), or those that are naturally sweet, fresh, and not burnt are recommended.

A man seeking an elixir (*rasāyana*) should never consume spoiled milk or anything that is unwholesome; thus spoke Āyurveda. (493) All varieties of flowers and fruits, sweet meat, and sugar, when properly cooked and well-digested, are declared the best for an elixir. (494) They say that the milk of a black cow with her calf, boiled with water, increases strength, is aphrodisiac, and is declared the best for an elixir. (495)

One who consumes the essence of mercury (rasendra) should always drink well-boiled cow’s milk—its water having been evaporated by fire until it is cool—and mixed with sugar or granulated sugar. Water is considered to be of eight delightful types: celestial, atmospheric, mountain-born, well-water, that which arises from the surface of a broken rock, pond-water, lake-water, and spring-water. Among these, the water from King Champaka’s exceptionally pure and cool wells, stirred by various pleasant breezes and free from defects, is most excellent for consumption at night.

One who consumes meat should drink excellent, very cold water scented with aromatic herbs and grains. One should perform anointing (udvartana) with the oil of *balā* known as Śrī-Nārāyaṇa, or another oil, using powders ground from the two types of *vajra*. After food is well-digested, one who eats meat should quickly bathe with pleasantly warm water; this destroys Vāta, Pitta, and Kapha, bestows strength, improves the skin and complexion, and promotes corpulence.

It illuminates the form, pacifies the mind, increases passion, captivates the hearts of women, removes fatigue from the body, and facilitates the movement of rasa (mercury). (500) We shall now explain other applications of *rasendra* (mercury) that grant wealth and the perfection of the body. Regarding this, two verses must first be studied for the purpose of examining the "dead" [substance]: "Just as teeth do not become white like the pollen of the *ketakī* flower, so too the powders of mercury, the secondary minerals (*uparasa*), and metals are not fit for use [if they have not been properly processed]. (501)

1. "pākayuktamarjīṇa" kha || 2. “akṛṣṇāyā” ga | 9. *Dhūnijanādeya* | 6. *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā* | [Chapter] Herbs grown on anthills, wells, at the foot of trees, on roads, in temples, or in cremation grounds—even if extracted according to the prescribed rite—will not grant success. ||502|| Now, for the sake of killing mercury (*rasendra*) so that it may be fit for all medicinal applications, we shall describe the *Śāmbhavī Mudrā*: Heat below, water above, with sulphur and mercury in the middle.

If the *mudrā* is very firm, even one of meager fortune attains success. (503) If the medicinal powder (*kāryema*) is deficient there, then one should mix it with clay. When the fragrance is equal [to the other ingredients], it destroys diseases; when double, it conquers *rājayakṣman*. (504) When the three qualities of fragrance have decayed, it destroys the pride of women; when fourfold, one becomes radiant and an expert in all scriptures. (505) When fivefold, one becomes a perfected being (*siddha*); when sixfold, one becomes a conqueror of death. Thus it has been stated.

The ash-extract of sulphur (gandha) should be ground twice with the water of a virgin girl for a hundred times. Having sealed it in a small crucible (laghupuṭa), one should cook it; then, having extracted it, one should eat one niṣka with honey and clarified butter. This "Gandhāmṛta" elixir destroys old age and death. One should powder Bhūrāja root along with its roots, dried in the shade. An equal amount of Triphalā powder and sugar equal to the total weight [of the previous ingredients] should be added. One should consume one Pala of this after [the main medicine]; it removes death and old age within a year. Thus ends the Gandhāmṛta Rasa.

One should prepare one-quarter part gold ash from dead mercury (mṛtasūta). Mixed with milk, ghee, and honey, one should have [the patient] lick one māṣa in a vessel of kāntaloha; this destroys old age and death. One should daily lick one karṣa of bākucī powder soaked in the juice of dhātrī fruit as an after-drink (anupāna); thus the *hemasundara-rasa* is perfected. Thus ends the *Hemasundara-rasa*. [Note: 1.
