63. One *māṣa* of this mercury (*rasa*), taken for three days with the juice of *luṅga*, water, and *lavaka* leaves, and mixed with honey and clarified butter, destroys the entire multitude of diseases. It diminishes old age in a single year and bestows nourishment upon the body. This glorious mercury, called *Mṛtyuñjaya*, delights even a hundred women; who else is capable of describing its boundless power as it has been described by the Lord of the Mountains? (512–513)

"Luṅgāmbholavakadaleita" means that one should grind it for three days after adding drops of citron juice (*mātuluṅga-drava*) bit by bit. Thus ends the *Mṛtyuñjaya-rasa*. Having thoroughly ground pure mercury with an equal amount of poison for one *prahara*, place that mass in a beautiful golden vessel. Suspended in a *dolā* (swinging apparatus), wash it for a day in the liquid of *viṣamuṣṭi*; then repeat this process here twice more. When its essence has been extracted, skillfully reduce it to ash along with an amount of fragrance equal to the [original] pair of Śiva’s eyes.

One part of *vaikrānta* ash, one-half part each of *jayapāla* and *navāśaka*, and all poisons doubled in quantity, should be rubbed together in a mortar for three days with the juice of *kanaka-bhṛṅga*. Having thoroughly pressed it onto the surface of a vessel containing poisonous incense, it should be made loose with *bhṛṅga* juice and filled into a small glass jar, which is then sealed with cloth and placed in a sand-bath apparatus (*sikatā-yatra*). Once observed [to be processed], it should be ground and used in medicinal formulations in a dose of one *śāli* grain.

Give the *ānanda-sūta* (mercury of bliss), which is a lion-pot for all diseases, together with half a *gadyāṇaka* of white [sulfur] (517). O King of Physicians, whiten the directions with the nails of the Lord of Physicians using the luster of the shimmering moon; assume this title! (518). Thus, "twice" means one should perform everything as before twice; this is the sense. With the pair of eyes of Giriśa (Śiva), take six-fold sulfur; "by skillful means" refers to [placing it] in a glass flask (*kācakūpī*) and so forth. This is the *ānanda-srutarasa*.

One should grind mercury (sūta) mixed with sulphur (gandha) and magnetite (kāntapāṣāṇa) along with the seeds of *Brāhmī* for one day. Having formed a ball and coated it with borax (ṭaṅkaṇa), one should subsequently heat it in a cow-dung fire. When dried, if it falls as a metallic essence (sattva) into the primary dross (kiṭṭa), the mercury certainly attains a bound state (baddhatā). Once bound, by the application of alkali and glass (kāca), one should cause the mercury to circulate until it becomes equal to gold. When this pill (khoṭa) is placed in the mouth for half a year, it destroys all diseases and bestows happiness.

Alternatively, having boiled a *golaka* in milk, one should administer that milk with long peppers (*pippalī*) for consumption. Having cooked it in an iron vessel, it should be given in cases of dry anemia (*śuṣka-pāṇḍu*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), and diseases of the *pitta*. For wind disorders (*vāta*), one should cook the *golaka* in *vyoṣa-vātāri-taila* and administer the oil mixed with fragrant substances. To alleviate phlegm (*śleṣman*), one should cook the *golaka* in the juices of *bhārgī*, *muṇḍī*, *kāsamarda*, and *āṭarūṣa*. In cases of cough and asthma, one should administer that decoction mixed with honey and long pepper powder. Whichever [ingredient] is used for whichever disease...

A decoction is also mentioned; having cooked the *gola* (pill-mass) in that decoction, one should administer it for the destruction of various diseases—whatever has been proclaimed as beneficial for each specific ailment. This *prāṇikalpadruma-gola-rasa* has been described; having performed worship, one should employ it through the yoga of devotion. The meaning is that after first ensuring its capacity to withstand fire by means of skillful technique, one should subsequently burn it. Thus ends the *prāṇikalpadruma-gola-rasa*. One should grind mercury, sulfur, and copper with the juice of *sinduvāra* for one day in the sun; thereafter, [the mixture] should be placed within a *vālukāyantra* (sand-oven).

525–526. One should seal the crucible and cook it with a fierce fire for three *yāmas*. That *guñjā* [dose], together with a piece of *parṇa*, should be administered in all diseases. It should be given for the purpose of purifying the body, as well as for nourishment, virility, and strength. (*Induvārā* is called *nirguṇḍī* in the vernacular. Thus ends the *Trinetrarasa*. 527. One should grind purified sulfur, double the amount of mercury, for one day. For each metal, one should add an equal amount of refined, purified, and calcined metal.

Brāhmī, jayantī, nirguṇḍī, viṣamuṣṭi, punarnavā, nīlikā, girikarṇikā, kṛṣṇadhattūra, barley (yava), aṭarūṣa, and kākamācī—one should grind [the medicine] with the juices of these. One should administer three or four *guñjā* seeds for all diseases. One should drink it with a vehicle (anupāna) prescribed for the specific disease, or lukewarm water. [The preparation of] the eight metals (*aṣṭaloha*) is as follows: one part of mercury (*sūta*) and eight parts of iron (*loha*). This is the Śārdūla-rasa.

Take one-sixth part of *meghabhasma* (ash of clouds) and five parts of pure *gandha* (sulfur). One should separately saturate [the mixture] seven times with the juices of *śigru*, *vahni* (*citronella*), and *kaṭukī*. One should always consume a *niṣka* measure of this; it thoroughly destroys old age and death. By consuming this "Ocean of Nectar" elixir for four months, one attains the lifespan of Brahmā. Afterwards, one should eat sesame seeds and *koraṇṭa* leaves with jaggery. *Koraṇṭa* is known in the vernacular as *kaṇṭasaireyā*. Thus ends the "Ocean of Nectar" elixir.

Equal to the powder of the aphrodisiac group (*vṛṣyagaṇa*), with that *puṭapāka* [preparation] and double the amount of sugar—this "jewel of powders" (*cūrṇaratna*) is a supreme aphrodisiac, even more potent than other aphrodisiacs, and a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*). (535) Now, he describes the powder of the aphrodisiac group beginning with *śatāvarī*: *śatāvarī*, *vidārī*, *gokṣura*, *ikṣuraka*, *vānarī*, *balā*, black and white *musalī*, *mistrī*, seeds of *ikṣuraka*, and *atibalā*—this is the aphrodisiac group (*vṛṣyagaṇa*). Here, the southerners add mercury (*rasa*) perfumed with fragrances, as well as mica (*abhra*) and other minerals.

This is the jewel-like powder known as *rasāyana*; milk and other liquids are to be taken as after-drinks (*anupeya*). [From the] *Āyurvedīya-granthamālā*, volume 66. Poison, the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*), *mustā*, turmeric, neem sprouts, and *viḍaṅga* as the eighth—these powders, each in equal parts, should be mixed with goat’s urine. A pill the size of a chickpea, which is a vehicle for the application of the medicine, is called *jayā*. Thus ends the *jayā-vaṭī*. Sulphur and iron ash, combined with honey and clarified butter, should be consumed in a dose of one *karṣa* with water infused with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).

"When the hair is bright and black, divine vision, nourishment, and valor arise from *gandhaloha*. Thus ends the section on *gandhaloha*. "Having processed [the mercury] eight times in gold and silver, and sixteen times in the [flesh of] a peacock and a rat, increasing it step by step; then, placing the vessel above milk and below fire, O wise ones, achieve complete and incomparable perfection in your own hands. (538) The phrase "eight parts" (*aṣṭāṃśa*) is illustrative; it may even be increased up to a hundredfold. Equal parts of mercury, sulfur, iron, and mica, along with gold, are to be combined with the quicksilver.

Having indeed cast all [the ingredients] into a mortar and crushed them with the juice of *kanyā*, one should wrap them in castor leaves (*eraṇḍapatra*) and place them on a heap of grain for three days. Having then extracted that [mixture], one should employ it against all diseases. This [preparation] is a fierce subduer of consumption; when combined with *triphalā* and honey, it cures the eleven types of wasting disease (*kṣaya*), the five types of cough, the eighteen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and various forms of jaundice and urinary disorders (*prameha*).

When practiced in sequence, it destroys dyspnea, weak digestion, hiccup, and acid bile; all types of ulcers, *āḍhyavāta*, erysipelas (*visarpa*), and abscesses (*vidradhi*); *apasāra*, seizures, insanity, and all skin diseases—just as Indra’s thunderbolt destroys a tree. [From the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*: It is nourishing, promotes longevity, and is the cause for the birth of sons; it was taught by the four-faced Lord to Kṛṣṇātreya. Thus ends the "Four-Faced Elixir" (*caturmukharasa*).

Thus ends the first chapter, on the preparation of minerals (*sūtasādhana*), in the *Āyurvedaprakāśa* composed by Upādhyāya Mādhava, the ornament of the Sārakhata lineage born in the land of Saurāṣṭra. Now begins the second chapter: Next, the minor minerals (*uparasas*) are described. They are: sulphur (*gandha*), realgar (*heṅgula*), mica (*abhra*), orpiment (*tālaka*), mica-slate (*śilā*), antimony (*srotoñjana*), borax (*ṭaṅkaṇa*), rājāvarta, magnetite (*cumbaka*), rock crystal (*sphaṭikā*), conch-shell (*śaṅkha*), chalk (*khaṭī*), and red ochre (*gairika*).

Copper sulfate (kāsīsa), green vitriol (rasaka), cowrie shells, sand, bolā, aśvakarṇa, kaṭuṣṭha, and saurāṣṭrī—these are considered minor minerals (uparasas) because they possess certain qualities similar to those of mercury. If these are purified according to the prescribed method and properly processed, when administered with appropriate adjuncts (anupāna) that alleviate specific diseases, they bestow long life. Now, O Śaṅkara, you should first describe the origin and the method of purification of sulfur (gandhaka), together with its names and characteristics.

Īśvara said: "O Goddess, in ancient times on the shore of the Ocean of Milk in Śvetadvīpa, as you were sporting with your companions, your menstrual flow occurred. That flow was abundant, exceedingly fragrant, and most enchanting. While you were bathing in the Ocean of Milk, your silken garment became stained with that flow; when it was washed by your companions, that flow turned into the substance known as Gandhaka. Furthermore, this very substance emerged along with the nectar (amṛta) during the churning of the Ocean of Milk."

Gladdening all those gods and Dānavas with its own fragrance, it was then said by the hosts of gods: "Let this be named Gandhaka. [6] It gladdened the Dānavas... [67] ...Āyurvedīyagranthamālā. [Chapter] "May this serve for the binding and the digestion (jāraṇā) of mercury; may whatever qualities are proclaimed of pārada also exist here. [7] Thus, this is renowned on the circle of the earth by the name Gandhaka.

Formerly, Bali resorted to it for the sake of attaining great strength. As Vāsuki was being pulled by him, a substance rich with the scent of sulphur (gandhaka) issued forth from every part of his body, driven out by the flames from his mouth. Because it attained the state of *gandha* (fragrance/sulphur), it is known as *balivasā*. Now, the names of *gandhaka*: *Gandhaka*, *Gandhika*, *Gandhapāṣāṇa*, *Saugandhika*, *Bali*, and also *Balivasā*. Now, the nature of *gandhaka*.

Sulfur is said to be of four types: red, yellow, white, and black. The red variety is prescribed for gold-making; that which resembles the beak of a parrot is the best. The yellow variety, known as *āmalasāra*, is excellent for mercury-based elixirs (*rasāyana*). Here, the white variety is called *khaṭikā*; it is used for plastering and for the killing of metals, as well as for plastering wounds and the like. Now, the qualities of pure sulfur are described: it is difficult to find in its black form, yet it destroys old age and death. Sulfur is a supreme elixir (*atirasāyana*).

Gandhaka (sulphur) produced from Gaurī flowers is indeed equally pungent, hot in its post-digestive effect (*vipāka*), and acrid; it destroys itching, leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), erysipelas (*visarpa*), and *dadru* skin diseases. It is an inflamer (*saṃdīpana*), a digestive (*pācana*), a loosener of undigested matter (*āmamonmocana*), a desiccant, an antidote to poison, and possesses the potency of mercury (*sūtendra*). It likewise destroys worms, is of the nature of *sattva*, and overcomes *chardi* (vomiting). Furthermore, another type of gandhaka is pungent, bitter, hot in potency, astringent, and laxative. It increases *pitta*, is acrid in its post-digestive effect, and conquers itching, erysipelas, and parasites. It cures leprosy, consumption (*kṣaya*), splenic disorders (*plīha*), and disorders of *kapha* and *vāta*; it is a rejuvenator (*rasāyana*). (13–14)

The Light of Āyurveda. 69. Now, the qualities of purified sulfur: Purified sulfur removes diseases such as leprosy, death, and old age; it generates fire, is greatly heating, and increases virility and strength. 15. Now, the defects of unpurified sulfur: Impure sulfur causes leprosy, fever, vertigo, and likewise diseases of bile (pitta); it destroys complexion, happiness, virility, and strength; therefore, it should be employed only when thoroughly purified. 16. Now, the purification of sulfur is described.

Sulfur kept in a vessel containing milk becomes pure when placed in cloth after being processed in a tortoise-shaped crucible; or likewise, it attains purity when placed in sour gruel (kāñjika) or in ghee. Now, the characteristics of sulfur fit for purification: Sulfur that has a luster like a parrot’s wing, a brilliance like fresh butter, and is smooth, hard, and glossy, is said to be the best. Now, purification according to another opinion: One should place ghee in an iron vessel and heat it over a fire.

One should add an equal amount of sulphur powder to that melted ghee. Having ascertained that the sulphur has been dissolved, one should place it in a thin cloth so that it all falls into the milk after being extracted from the cloth. Once cooled, removed, and washed, one should dry it with a cloth. When thus rendered pure, the sulphur is said to be purified. In this manner, it should be diligently purified three times by means of milk.

Vāgbhaṭa states the purpose of straining it through a cloth for the sake of consumption by physicians and for medicinal formulations: "Thus purified, this [mercury] casts stones into the sky; in ghee, it takes the form of chaff, and it attains a state of solid globules on its own. Now, the purification by means of the *kūrmapuṭa* (tortoise-oven) is explained clearly: having poured milk into a vessel containing clarified butter, one should seal the mouth with a cloth. *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter [Number].

[All] names: No cause. One should swallow sulphur (gandhaka) that has been ground into a fine powder. One should cover the sulphur with a wide and long earthen pan (kharpara). A seal must be made at the joint between the vessel and the pan by means of clay. Having placed the vessel in a hole in the ground, one should leave its mouth slightly exposed. One should ignite a fire above the pan using flint stones (vanopala). Then, the sulphur, having melted in milk, should be cooled and washed with water.

26. One should employ sulphur that has been rubbed with cloth and dried in the absence of water as pure for spiritual practices (*yoga*). According to another opinion, sulphur melted and thrown into the juice of *bhṛṅga* becomes purified; thus seven times for the purpose of making it fine, but only once for the purpose of [medicinal] application. 27. Thus purified, sulphur does not undergo transformation through unwholesome substances (*apathya*); otherwise, due to unwholesomeness, it would kill like the *hālāhala* poison when drunk. 28. Now, regarding the preparation of sulphur—the method for destroying the odor of sulphur: having powdered it, one should cook it in the milk of *gandhūka* until it reaches the state of thickening.

Then, having added the juice of *sūryāvarta* again, one should cook it slowly. Afterwards, the wise person should pour it into water produced from the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). Once the sulphur has lost its own characteristic smell, it is known as purified. Now, regarding the methods of consuming sulphur: thus purified, [the sulphur] measuring one *śāṇa*, when licked together with *triphalā*, clarified butter, *bhṛṅgarāja*, and honey—

It makes the pair of eyes equal to those of a vulture and brings about a long life free from disease. (31) Here, the wholesome diet is milk with rice. Thus ends the ritual procedure for sulphur (*gandhakakalpa*). One *niṣka* of purified sulphur, taken with milk for a month, increases valor and virility. After six months, there is the destruction of all diseases, divine vision, long life, and a beautiful form. (32) Thus ends the second ritual procedure for sulphur. [From the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*, 72]

Now, regarding *gandhataila* (fragrant oil): one should add the powder of *gandhaka* (sulfur) to milk that is being boiled. This *gandhataila*, when combined with clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), cures [skin diseases]. *Gandhataila* destroys *galatkuṣṭha* (oozing leprosy) through both external application and internal consumption. Having carefully ground five *palas* of *gandhāsmana* (sulfur) into a fine powder, it should be thoroughly mixed with three times as much *mārkaṇḍī* juice and dried in the shade.

A person who consumes one *pala* each of these—mercury powder (*yatkhācūrṇa*), *abhayā*, honey, and ghee—as a linctus every day for two months, attains youth even if aged. Thus ends the third section on the ritual of sulphur (*gandhakakalpa*). The man who daily drinks one *karṣa* of powdered sulphur with oil, remaining devoted to the application of warm water [for bathing] at the proper time every day, destroys all diseases such as scabies (*pāmā*) within three weeks. By virtue of constant practice, he becomes free from all afflictions and distress.

Thus ends the fourth formulation of sulphur (*gandhakakalpa*). Furthermore, one of fierce intellect who has honored his guru, who is devoted to the worship of Bhūteśa (Śiva), and who consumes this well-ground sulphur in equal parts with black iron-sulphide (*kṛṣṇā*) and *pathyā* (harītakī), shall be free from ailments such as hemorrhoids and the like; he will possess abundant nourishment and virility, and will shine with the luster of gold, his pair of lotus-like eyes fully blossomed. (35) Thus ends the fifth formulation of sulphur (*gandhakakalpa*). Pure sulphur, combined with *kalāśa*, *vyoṣa*, and well-ground [other ingredients], [should be used].

Having scattered that [substance] upon a cloth measuring one *aratni* in length, one should wrap it; then, having bound it with a thread, one should immerse it in oil for a watch (*yāma*). Holding the wick (*varti*) with tweezers, one should ignite it in the middle. The liquid essence (*druta*) that falls drop by drop should be caught in a glass vessel. One should place that liquid into a leaf of the *nāgavallī*, adding three drops. [From the] *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*: [One should] triturate pure mercury (*sūtendra*) measured by a *vatsa*.

One should consume that mercury along with the leaf-vein [of the plant] using a finger; it produces intense digestive stimulation (dīpana) and destroys consumption (kṣaya), jaundice (pāṇḍu), emaciation (kārsa), asthma (śvāsa), the pain of colic (śūla), and even difficult-to-cure dysentery (grahaṇī). It quickly destroys undigested matter (āma) and brings about lightness of the body. Thus ends the sixth procedure for sulphur (gandhakakalpa). Furthermore, purified [mercury] should be processed three times with the milk of *balēya* and then four times with water containing *guḍūcī*.

It should be processed eight times separately with the waters of *pathyā*, *akṣadhātrī*, medicinal herbs, and *bhṛṅga*, as well as with fresh ginger (*ārdraka*). Once prepared, add an equal portion of sugar; this elixir (*rasāyana*) shall be known by the name *Gandharkeśa*. It wards off the depletion of bodily tissues (*dhātu-kṣaya*), the group of urinary disorders (*meha*), weak digestion, colic, diseases located in the abdominal cavity, the eighteen types of leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), and indeed all collections of diseases, including those of kings.

By consuming [this] for half a karṣa, a mortal attains virility, nourishment, strength, and the brilliance of the digestive fire (agni-dīpti). (43) First, one should prepare the body through emetics and purgatives; then one should employ the meat of wild animals (jāṅgala) and that of goats. (44) Likewise, one should avoid salty and sour vegetables, pulses (dvidala), women, riding, and vehicles at all times. (45) Thus ends the excellent and universal procedure for the Gandhaka-rasāyana, combined with Vātāri-taila and Triphalā-kauśika.

Sulfur combined with mercury destroys old age and disease. (46) Listen, I shall describe its qualities: through practice for only one month, all diseases—hemorrhoids, fistula-in-ano, and those arising from phlegm—are destroyed by sulfur in a single month. By practicing it for six months, a man becomes equal to a god. (47–48) [From the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*: "It quickly dries up the body. [Variants: 1. *viśoṣayatyāśu gā*; 2. *vibhāvya ga*; 3. *gandhakasajñaka ga*.]

73. Those whose hair is the color of a swan, whose eyebrows are long-hanging, whose teeth are loose, and whose vision is dull, suffer from the depletion of strength, semen, and other vital fluids. Having conquered youth, they go [to old age] with hair like bees. One who possesses divine vision and great vitality has ears like those of a boar; he is equal to Tārkṣya (Garuḍa) in his gaze and possesses the strength and prowess of a powerful one. With firm teeth and a body like a diamond, he is like a second Viṣṇu. By his urine and excrement, the earth becomes gold.

The eighth [chapter], the *Gandhakakalpa* (The Alchemical Preparation of Sulphur): One *pala* of sulphur and half a *pala* of mercury should be rubbed with the juice of *kumārī* for one day and formed into a ball (*golaka*). Placed in an *andhamūṣā* crucible and heated by blowing, it should be licked with honey and clarified butter. By using this for only a month, old age and poverty are destroyed. Thus ends the ninth [chapter], the *Gandhakakalpa*. One should prepare equal parts of *triphalā*, sulphur, and *bhṛṅgarāja*. By using this for one year, one may live as long as the moon, the sun, and the stars.

Thus ends the tenth *gandhaka*-kalpa. One should drink one *pala* of sulphur mixed with milk. By practicing this for a year, one shall live as long as the moon, sun, and stars, becoming irresistible to all beings like a second Śaṅkara. (55) Thus ends the eleventh *gandhaka*-kalpa. One should plaster a cloth seven times with the milk of a camel and the milk of a *khuhū* cow; then, having ground sulphur with butter, one should smear it upon the cloth. (56)

A wick made from that [substance] smeared with *daṃśa* ghee should be held with its tip facing downward; the oil that drips into the vessel below should be collected and employed in medicinal formulations. Thus ends the *Gandhakataila*. [In the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter on Sulfur: Sulfur combined with an equal amount of black pepper, along with *ṣuṅgu*, *triphala*, and *śamyāka* root decoction, when processed [in this way], destroys all diseases. Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the *Gandhakakalpa*.

Excellent sulphur, rubbed with the bitter juices of *imiyāka* roots, when applied to the body certainly destroys scabies, leprosy, ringworm, and other such ailments. (59) Thus ends the thirteenth chapter on sulphur, concerning *kaṇḍūlī*. Two *niṣkas* of purified sulphur, mixed with oil, and subsequently with black pepper, oil, and the juice of *apāmārga*, should be ground together. This paste should then be diligently smeared over the entire body of the patient. The patient should then remain in the heat [of the sun] at midday and consume curd-rice (*takrabhakta*). (60–61)

One should eat at night and consume [the medicine] with fire [as a digestive aid]; having risen in the morning, one should smear the body with the dung of a buffalo and a goat and perform a bath. By means of cold water, scabies (pāmā), itching (kharju), and leprosy (kuṣṭha) are pacified. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter on sulphur (gandhaka) for the treatment of scabies, itching, leprosy, and so forth. Thus ends the second chapter in the *Āyurvedaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Mādhava, the ornament of the Sārakhata clan born in the land of Sorāṣṭra. Now begins the third chapter.

Now, the names, characteristics, qualities, origins, and purification of *darada* (cinnabar): *Hijula*, *darada*, *mlecha*, *heku*, *lavūrṇa*, *pārada-mūla*, *suraṅga*, *rasagarbha*, *babara*, and also *rakta*. (1) *Cinnabar* (*darada*) is said to be of three types: *camīra*, *śukatuṇḍaka*, and *haṃsapāda*; each subsequent one is superior in quality. (2) *Camīra* is yellowish-white; *śukatuṇḍaka* is like the beak of a parrot; *haṃsapāda*, which resembles the *japā* flower, is the most excellent. (3)
3] Āyurvedaprakāśa | U9'A Qualities: Bitter, astringent, and pungent; it is difficult to digest, cures eye diseases, and removes phlegm and bile.

It destroys nausea, leprosy, fever, jaundice, hemorrhoids, splenic disorders, āma-vāta, and artificial poison (gara). Now, the defects of impure cinnabar (darada): Impure cinnabar may cause blindness, emaciation, exhaustion, vertigo, delusion, and urinary disorders (meha); therefore, mercury (heṅgula) must be thoroughly purified by physicians. The purification of cinnabar (heṅgula): Cinnabar, processed with sheep’s milk and sour gruel (amlavarga), certainly attains purity after being treated diligently seven times. —Vāgbhaṭa.

Having been dried seven times with the juice of *ārdraka* (ginger), *drava* (juice), *elā* (cardamom), *kha* (salt?), *ambu* (water), or even [other liquids], and having been processed (*bhāvita*), it indeed becomes free from defects. Now, the process of killing (*māraṇa*): Having placed it inside a thin cloth and a *kakṣuka* (a type of vessel or container), and having placed it within the bulb of a *paṭarañjana* plant, one should wrap it completely with clay and roast it by the method of *puṭapāka* using ten *vanopalas* (forest stones). In this manner, one should perform a hundred roasts; then likewise a hundred roasts with *vanavṛntāka* (wild eggplant); then a hundred roasts with *mandāra* fruit. Then...

In this manner, one hundred folds [of the leaf] of *indravāruṇī* fruit; then, one hundred folds of *amlavetasa* fruit. Thereupon, it becomes perfected and turns a pale red color. One should consume one *raktikā* of this with a piece of sugar-candy, along with fragrant substances such as the "three aromatics" (*trigandha*) as available. It possesses double the digestive fire and double the capacity for desire, and brings about the destruction of cough, asthma, consumption, fever, and so forth. It is bitter and hot, a divine substance produced from mercury and sulfur.

It destroys urinary disorders and leprosy, improves appetite, provides strength, and increases intellect and digestive fire. Now follows the purification of *hiṅgula* (mercuric oxide), which is described as being included in the *Sūpad-dhati*: One part of impure mercury and four parts of sulfur—having cast both into an iron vessel, one should cook them for a moment over a mild fire. (5) Into that [mixture], one should add the powder of *manaḥśilā* (realgar) amounting to one-tenth of the mercury. (76) [From the *Āyurvedīya-granthamālā*, Chapter *...*]

Having cast it into a crucible and stirred it well, one should remove it once it has become thoroughly cooled. Then, having broken it into pieces and sealed them in a glass flask (kācakūpī), one should properly coat the glass flask with a medicinal paste (vasūtikā). Enclosing it with a thickness of one finger-breadth, one should let it dry in the shade. Then, one should cook it for one day over a mild fire inside a sand-bath apparatus (vālukāyantra). Afterwards, one should cook it for five days over a gradually increasing heat. Having extracted it after seven days, it becomes the excellent *heṅgula* vermilion.

Furthermore, mercury processed in a *ḍamaru* apparatus by means of upward sublimation (*ūrdhvapātana*) and purified cinnabar (*hiṅgula*) that has been distilled—this indeed requires no further purification. Having rubbed it for one *yāma* with lime juice or the juice of *nimba* leaves, one should cause it to fall upward from a great height according to the method of distillation. There, one should collect the excellent liquid clinging to the upper vessel; for this mercury is indeed pure and may be employed in all operations.

Indeed, in the treatises on mercury (rasatantra), the purification of *hiḍḍulaka* alone is mentioned, and no other procedure; this is the general direction. Thus ends the third chapter in the *Āyurvedaprakāśa* composed by the illustrious Mādhava, the ornament of the Sārakhata lineage. Now begins the fourth chapter. Hereafter, I shall explain this chapter concerning mica (*abhraka*). Formerly, for the sake of slaying Vṛtra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra) raised his vajra. From that [vajra], sparks were scattered throughout the sky. (1)

They fell with a deep roar upon the peaks of the great mountains; from those very peaks, various types of *abhra* (mica) were produced. (2) Because it is born from the thunderbolt (*vajra*) and because it arises from the sound of the whirling clouds, and since it fell from the sky, it is therefore considered *bhṛṅgaṇa*. (3) Due to the divisions of Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra, it is of four kinds; in order, it is white, red, yellow, and black by color. (4)

White *sita* is praised for *tāra* (silver); red, for *rasāyana* (alchemy/elixirs); yellow, for gold; and black, for diseases as well as for liquefaction (*druti*). || 5 || It is of four kinds: *pināka*, *dardura*, *nāga*, and *vajra*. The wise have described *kṛṣṇāśru* as their characteristic; its definition is stated as follows: || 6 || If one ignorant[ly] throws *pināka* into a heap of leaves, it sheds tears [black smoke]; that ignorance bestows great leprosy (*mahākuṣṭha*) upon him. || 7 || *Dardura*, when thrown into fire, makes a croaking sound like a frog.

Having made many pellets from it, one should blow upon a snake-like [substance] in the fire like a snake; that which is consumed by it certainly produces fistula (bhagaṇdar). But the *vajra* [mineral], like a thunderbolt, does not undergo transformation even when cast into the fire. O best of those with clouds [of merit], this *vajra* conquers disease, old age, and death. Also elsewhere: "When it is thrown into the fire like collyrium, it does not undergo transformation."

Indeed, that mica which is as hard as a diamond is suitable for all purposes, and nothing else. (11) Mica originating from the northern mountain possesses abundant *sattva* and superior qualities; that produced from the southern mountain has little *sattva* and inferior qualities. (12) Regarding the selection of mica: "Mica should be extracted by physicians from a mine and crushed to the size of a man; it yields results according to its weight and its *sattva*, while that which is otherwise possesses fewer qualities. (13) [Variant reading: 'mica originating from the eastern mountain']

V5: The pair of rītikās (brass and bronze) is dry, bitter, and salty in taste; it is purifying, cures anemia and worms, and is not excessively scraping. Its ash, when consumed together with the powder of *nimba* (eightfold), *bhallātaka*, sesame, *brahmabīja*, *ajamodā*, and *agni*, becomes a destroyer of parasites and a remover of white leprosy (*śvetakuṣṭha*). [155 12] *Āyurvedaprakāśa*.

When brass-dust is eaten by a goat for an indefinite period, its excrement should be written upon a shallow pan (kharpara). After that pan has been heated, it emits brass. Having collected that brass and processed it, one should fashion a seal-ring (mudrikā) and wear it; it becomes equal in quality to fourteen-carat gold. Now, for the purification and smelting of both [gold and brass]: one should heat the leaves made of the two, namely copper and brass, and repeatedly drench them while they are hot in oil and sour gruel (kāñjika). (71)

By immersing brass and bronze three times each in cow urine and three times each in a decoction of *kulattha* beans, their purification is thoroughly accomplished. (72) As for specific purification: an intelligent person should cook brass leaves in cow urine for one *yāma* over a steady fire; once cooked, they are purified even when placed in sour substances. (73) Bronze, when heated and quenched in the juice of *nirguṇḍī* mixed with the powder of *śyāmā*, attains purity; or it may be purified by being cooked in sour substances as well. (74)

Now, for the killing [of metals]: one should grind sulphur with the milk of *arka* and smear it [upon the metal]. Pure bell-metal leaves should be repeatedly washed with acidic liquids using an equal amount [of the paste]. Then, having placed them in a clay crucible (*mṛṣāpuṭa*), one should perform a *puṭapāka* using a *raja-puṭa*. By means of two such *puṭas*, bell-metal and brass are certainly killed. One should purify bell-metal and royal brass (*rājarīti*) in the same manner as copper; the killing of these two has also been described by the best of physicians in the same way as that of copper.

Now, *bhartasaṃśa* (the bearer) is an alloy of five metals (*pañcaloha*) known by the name *pañcara*; it is a secondary metal (*adhi-kopadhātu*). Just as brass (*kāṃsya*) and pewter (*rīti*), so too are tin (*tāja*), lead (*nāga*), and mercury (*vaṅga*) as the fifth. When these are melted together in one place, *pañcaloha* is produced. [From the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter 156: *Pañcaloha* consists of five metals and five tastes; it is circular and is also called *bhartra*. Its appearance and other characteristics are distinct; when prepared in a vessel, it is auspicious.

First, the five metals (pañcaloha) should be purified in oil and other liquids, and subsequently poured into goat’s urine; they attain purity, of this there is no doubt. (80) By rubbing with sulphur and orpiment ground with the milk of the *arka* plant and heating in five *kumbha-puṭas*, the "carrier" (*yogavāhaka*) metal is killed. Thus ends the killing of the metals. All [metals] except for ghee should be cooked by the wise in a brass vessel; eating from it is recommended, while bell-metal (*rītikā*) is considered mediocre. (82) Now, regarding vermilion (*sindūra*).

Sindūra is red powder, and nāgagarbha is lead (sīsaka). Sindūra, which is a secondary derivative of lead, is considered by its qualities to be like lead itself. Other qualities of it are also recorded due to the power of its combination [with other substances]. Sindūra is hot; it destroys erysipelas, leprosy, itching, and poison. It promotes the healing of fractures and cleanses and heals wounds. Now, regarding purification: therein, the characteristics of sindūra suitable for purification are as follows: it should be brilliant, fire-resistant, unctuous, fine, clear, heavy, and difficult to grind.

Pure vermilion produced from a gold mine bestows auspiciousness; its purification through the application of milk and sour gruel has been declared by the wise. (85) According to another opinion: having ground the vermilion with the juice of *nimbuka* fruits, one should dry it in the sun; thereafter, it becomes purified by means of rice-water. (86) Indeed, the separate use of vermilion has not been observed anywhere; therefore, it should be employed in the aforementioned instances according to the instruction of the Guru. (87) [12] Āyurvedaprakāśa.

157. Now, the origin, characteristics, qualities, and purification of *śilājatu*: *Śilājatu* is said to be of two kinds; the first is produced from mountains (*girisaṃbhava*). The second arises from alkaline soil through the combination of earth and water. (88) Just as in the summer heat, mountains release the essence of their minerals like sap when scorched by the sun, that is celebrated as *śilājatu*. It is of four types: golden, silver, copper, and iron. (89)

Indeed, *śilājatu* (bitumen) should be recognized by its respective characteristics: that which is born from stone (*śailaja*) is golden in color, like the *japā* flower; it is sweet, pungent, bitter, cooling, and has a pungent post-digestive effect (*vipāka*). That which is silver-colored is cooling, pungent, and has a sweet post-digestive effect. That which resembles the neck of a peacock is called *tūphī*; it is sharp and hot. That which is born from iron resembles the color of a *jaṭāyu* bird; it is bitter and salty. It is pungent in its post-digestive effect and cooling; this is declared to be the best of all.

Furthermore: Iron that smells like cow’s urine, is black, soft, and heavy, and is bitter, astringent, and cold—such iron is the very best. (94) Regarding another characteristic: That which resembles guggulu resin, is bitter and salty, pungent in its post-digestive effect (vipāka), and cold—such iron is the very best. (95) Gold [iron] is for wind and bile (vātapitta); silver [iron] is for phlegm and bile (śleṣmapitta); copper [iron] is for diseases of phlegm; and iron produced from ore (lohaja) removes all three humors (tridoṣa). (96)

On the Vindhya mountain, iron (*lauha*) is found in great abundance; therefore, it is superior there. Without its purification, it is useless due to the accumulation of many impurities. [14–158] *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*. (Chapter) It is a rejuvenative (*rasāyana*) that is pungent, bitter, hot, and has a pungent post-digestive effect (*pāka*). It is beneficial for medicinal formulations (*yoga*) and destroys phlegm (*kapha*), urinary disorders (*meha*), stones (*aśman*), and gravel (*śarkarā*). [14–159] It cures dysuria (*sūtrakṛcchra*), consumption (*kṣaya*), asthma (*śvāsa*), anemia (*vātāmrā*), jaundice (*pāṇḍutā*), epilepsy (*apasmāra*), insanity (*unmāda*), edema (*śotha*), leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), abdominal enlargements (*udara*), and worms (*kṛmi*). [14–160]

The qualities of impure *śilājatu*: Impure *śilājatu* causes burning sensations, fainting, giddiness, hemorrhaging, and emaciation; it also produces sluggishness and aggravates the *malas*. (100) Now, the purification: Having obtained pure *śilājatu* possessing the characteristic marks of its metallic origin, one should wash it with plain water to remove the external impurities. (101) Next, Hārīta describes the method for destroying its internal impurities: One should properly soak it with iron filings, *nimba*, *guḍūcī*, clarified butter, and barley.

For the purpose of warding off the defects caused by *saṃtānikā*, insects, moths, gadflies, and poisonous herbs. (102) *Saṃtānikā* is foul clay mixed within [the medicine]. Regarding this, Vāgbhaṭa states the following procedure for the purpose of saturation (*bhāvanā*): "The medicinal drug to be saturated should be stated as equal to eight parts of water and the mountain-born [clay] (*girija*). When that decoction has been reduced to one-fourth, one should add the mountain-born [clay] while it is hot. Once it has reached a state of uniform consistency and is dried, one should again throw it back into the liquid. (103)

Thus, having spoken with each [patient] individually seven times, one should then proceed. Having thus applied the mental visualization (*bhāvanā*) and dried [the substance], the purification must be performed using pure water alone. Regarding that procedure, Agniveśa says: "In the hot season, when the sun's heat is intense, in a place free from drafts and on level ground, one should carefully place four vessels made of black iron in the sun. Having obtained the finest *śilājatu* and placed it in a vessel, one should add twice as much water."

Having added half of that [quantity] boiled until hot, one should purify it properly as it rises; having strained it through a fine cloth, it should be placed back again therein. Then, whatever black matter rises to the top like a film (saṃtānikā), heated by the rays of the sun, one should place that in another vessel; having placed lukewarm water within it, one should then [place it] from that vessel into yet another vessel. || 106–108 || *Āyurvedaprakāśa*, Chapter 159.

Then, having placed Kṛṣṇa elsewhere, one should again bring back that which was withdrawn. When the water has become pure and clear, and the impurity, due to its placid state, has settled at the bottom, then one should discard that water and the impurity; thus the water becomes purified like bitumen (śilājatu). Indeed, everything drawn from the fourth vessel is for the purpose of testing; I shall speak of this further. Just as when cast into fire it burns without smoke, and upon cooking it becomes like a Liṅga.

Like a thread dropped on water with a blade of grass, [the pure substance] sinks downwards; that which smells like cow’s urine, is dark, yet becomes clear, is to be known as *śilājatu*. (111) Thus have the methods of purification and its qualities been previously described. Now, the names: *śilājitu*, *indrajatu*, and also *śailaniryāsa*; it is also called *gaireya*, *aśmaja*, *girija*, and *śailadhātujam*. (112) Now, for the sake of urgent business, the abbreviated method of purification is as follows: *śilājatu* ground with cow’s milk, *triphalā*, and *bhṛṅgarāja*.

In a vessel made of iron, it undoubtedly attains purity in a single day. Thus ends the summary of purification. Now, for the excellence of its qualities, the purified *śilājatu* should be processed with the water of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*), cow’s milk, and cow’s urine. One should place a small amount according to the prescribed method in a glass vessel. One should diligently consume it with auspicious incenses such as *aguru* and others; thereafter, one who has been properly cleansed and lubricated should practice its use in the proper dosage according to the rules.

One *karṣa*, half a *pala*, and one *pala* for one, three, and seven weeks respectively, are considered the inferior, middling, and superior methods of using *śilāja* (bitumen). Stirred with milk, it quickly yields the fruits of rejuvenation (*rāsa-yana*); one who eats sparingly and moderately will destroy all diseases without exception. [From the *Āyurvedīya-granthamālā*, Chapter 16: If one consumes exercise, sunlight, wind, mental distress, heavy food, or pungent substances, one should avoid them for twice as long after the period of use has ended.

One should always avoid horse-gram (*kulattha*), *kākamācī*, and pigeons. One should drink rainwater, well-water, or water from a spring. (119) There is no curable disease on earth that this [medicinal substance], when properly administered according to the requirements of the season, would not forcibly conquer. When used by one established in health, it bestows abundant vigor. (120) When employed with all appropriate adjuncts in all diseases, it surely conquers those various ailments through regular practice; of this there is no doubt. (121)

Whatever qualities reside in mercury, the secondary minerals (uparasa), the six metals, the gems, and the base metals, they enter into the mineral *śilādhātu* out of a desire to conquer old age and death. Regarding its calcination (*bhasma*), it is stated in the *Rasapaddhati*: "The mineral *śilādhātu*, when enclosed with sulphur (*gandha*) and *tāla* along with the juice of *mātuluṅga*, is indeed killed by eight *giriṇḍaka* [puṭa] applications. As for its extraction of the essence (*satva*): "The mountain-born [mineral], ground with the group of fluxing agents (*drāvaṇavarga*) and sour liquids, is blown in the interior of a crucible (*mūṣā*) by means of *kokila* [coals]; thus it attains its essence."

Now, regarding the second type of *śilājatu* in the sequence of liquids: the second is known as *soraka*, which is white-colored *śilājatu*. When used in the proportions of fire (three) and arrows (five), it is beneficial for urinary disorders (*mūtrāmaya*). Furthermore, *śilājatu* that is pale, sandy in appearance, and resembles *kapardika* (cowrie shells) destroys dysuria (*mūtrakṛcchra*), urinary calculi (*aśmarī*), urinary disorders (*meha*), jaundice (*kāmalā*), and anemia (*pāṇḍu*).

In the *Rasapaddhati* itself it is recited: "That which is another white *śilājatu*, called 'the stimulator of fire' (*vahnayuttejana*), is indeed for those afflicted by urinary disorders. Regarding the term "stimulator of fire": that other white *śilājatu* is a stimulator of fire and an inflamer of fire. Here, "fire" is not to be understood as the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*), but rather as fire-weapons; it is an inflamer of fire therein, known in the world as "sorā," and it is employed in fire-arrows (projectiles) for the purpose of manufacturing the substance commonly known as "dārubāruda" or gunpowder.

Thus ends the commentary on the *Rasapaddhati* by Mahādeva [12] 161: "That which is processed and mixed with the water of cardamom attains purity; for this, neither killing (*māraṇa*) nor subduing (*pātana*) is prescribed by the wise. Its origin, however, arises from specific types of earth and specific types of water. This concludes the examination of the secondary minerals (*upadhātu*). Now, there is another secondary mineral known as *capala*.

As stated in the *Rasapaddhati*: "There are four types of mercury (capala) distinguished as white, black, yellow, and red; furthermore, during the month of Magha, there are two resembling blood and collyrium which become [mercury] quickly due to their origin from lac. The remaining two, however, are auspicious because they liquefy slowly; these two are purified sevenfold by being bound or immersed in the water of Kakavī, Bhakaja, and Jambhala. When combined with the first constituent part, they subsequently follow the yoga; those originating from honey and the earth are declared by the wise to be aphrodisiacs that remove defects."

The remaining two, the green and the white, are fruitless (*moghau*); the fortunate ones (*subhagau*) are the heaviest. Due to their primacy, they first become binders of mercury (*rasabandhakau*). The rest is clear. Elsewhere, Capala is also said to be of four kinds: white, black, reddish, and green. It leaps in fire like a frog; therefore it is called *capala*. Capala has the luster of crystal, possesses six properties, is glossy and heavy, cures the three *doṣas*, is highly aphrodisiac, and acts as a binder of mercury.

This *capala* is recited by some as *parasa*, and by others among the *rasas*. Then, having been rubbed with poisons (*viṣa*), secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*), and fermented grain-sour (*dhānyāmla*), it is placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated; it releases its essence (*sattva*) and performs its function. Thus ends the section on *capala*. Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Āyurvedaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Mādhava, the Upādhyāya and ornament of the Sārasvata family born in the land of Saurāṣṭra. Now, [the following concerns] the origin, characteristics, qualities, purification, and processing of the various gems. Furthermore, the types of jewels should be understood as those which effect the binding of mercury (*sūtabandha*), which sustain the bodies of men, and which destroy old age and disease. (1) The Etymology of "Ratna": All people who seek wealth find extreme delight in these; therefore, they are called *ratna* by those expert in the science of words (*śabdaśāstra*). (2)

Now, regarding the names of gems and the definition of their nature: the word *ratna* is used in the neuter, while *maṇi* is said to be masculine and also feminine. That [term] refers to a variety of stones, such as diamond (*vajra*) and the like. In the *Rasapaddhati*, nine various gems are mentioned: diamond, coral, pearl, emerald, lapis lazuli, hessonite, ruby, sapphire, and topaz.

Whatever other [gems] there may be here within the bounds of the three worlds, those who examine them clearly state that they have attained the status of "secondary gems" (*uparatna*) by name. Diamond (*vajra*) is *hīraka*; coral (*vidruma*) is *pravāla*; pearl (*mauktika*) is *muktā*; emerald (*marakata*) is *garuḍodra*, known in the vernacular as *pana*; lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) is *ciduramaṇi*; gomedaka is well-known by that very name; ruby (*māṇikya*) is *padmarāga*; sapphire (*harinīla*) is *indranīla*; topaz (*puṣpadṛṣat*) is *puṣparāga*. The rest is clear.

In the *Viṣṇudharmottara* as well: "Pearl, diamond, lapis lazuli, ruby, topaz, emerald, agate, sapphire, and likewise emerald; these nine, together with coral, are indeed the great gems. (5) Elsewhere, the secondary gems (*uparatna*) are mentioned: "Vaikrānta, sun-stone (*sūryakānta*), moon-stone (*candrakānta*), rājāvarta, that which is called lāla, and another known as peroja. (6) [From the] *Āyurvedaprakāśa*.

Pearls from oyster shells, those from conch shells, those born of coral, as well as blue, yellow, and other gems, and others that are indeed antidotes to poison; and those which are suppressors of fire and so forth—all these world-renowned gems are reckoned by experts among the secondary gems (uparatnas). Now, the names of the gems: diamond is *hīraka* in the masculine, *vajra* in the neuter, and it is also called *candra* and *maṇivara*; emerald is *gārutmata*, *marakata*, *aśmagarbha*, and *harinmaṇi*.

Māṇikya and padmarāga denote the ruby; it is also called śoṇarakta and lohita. Puṣparāga is the topaz (manumaṇi), which has the luster of Bṛhaspati (Vācaspati). Indranīla and nīla denote the sapphire. Gomeda is yellowish-red. Vaiḍūrya is the lapis lazuli, a gem that possesses the brilliance of the planet Ketu. Muktā, mauktika, and śauktika denote pearl, as does muktāphala. Pravāla is used for coral in both masculine and neuter genders, while vidruma is used only in the masculine.

Oyster shell, bone, elephant tusk, snake, fish, frog, bamboo, and [the horn of] the blue jay—these eight are declared to be the sources of excellent pearls. Now, the origin and characteristics of *vīra* (diamond): the thunderbolt (*vajra*) was produced from the bones of Dadhīci; its fragments scattered upon the earth are known as diamonds, and they are classified into four types. That which is white is called *dvija* (twice-born); that which is red is declared to be *kṣatriya*; that which is yellow is said to be *vaiśya*; and that which is black is designated as *śūdra*.

The *viśra* is declared to be the best among elixirs (*rasāyana*), bestowing all perfections; it is the *kṣatriya*, the destroyer of diseases, and the supreme remover of old age and death. The *vaiśya* is said to bestow wealth and likewise provide firmness to the body; the *śūdra* destroys diseases and effects the stabilization of youth. These are to be identified as female, male, or neuter by their characteristics: those that are well-rounded, full of fruit, endowed with luster, and very large. (From the Āyurvedic treatise.)

Those diamonds which are devoid of lines and spots are indeed masculine (puruṣa). Those endowed with lines and spots and having six corners are known as feminine (strī). Furthermore, those that are triangular or very elongated should be understood as neuter (napuṃsaka). Among all of them, the masculine are the best; they are the piercers and the binders of mercury. The feminine ones bestow beauty upon the body and grant happiness to women. The neuter ones, however, are devoid of potency, lacking desire, and bereft of luster.

Vīryas (virilizers) should be administered to women; one should employ klības (eunuchs) for those who are impotent. All [medicines] that increase strength and virility should be applied to men. (22) Now, the origin of diamonds is described differently according to the *Rasapaddhati*: "Formerly, a son of Diti named Bala was born, who was invincible to the three worlds. Then, by the gods, he was entreated with their whole being at a sacrifice to offer his body, and he became a diamond-bodied [jewel]."

Then, having made his own body free from pain, the wise one stood before the gods; he was then offered to the Lord of Birds by those who subsist on the seven sacrificial threads. Then Vīṇavī cut off his head with a thunderbolt-headed blade. Again, the ancient seers say that he was restored as Bala, a collection of jewels.

Those who were born from his mouth are remembered as the *śubhas* (the twice-born *brāhmaṇas*). Those who emerged from his arms are known as the *apsarases*, and they are the *kṣatriyas*. 24. Those who fell from his navel and his waist are named the *bhūmispṛśas* (the *vaiśyas*), and those who fell from both his knees and both his feet are considered the *śūdras*. 25. 165. This is clear. Here, the determination is made according to the different ages (*yuga*). Or, let it be that [diamonds] arise from three sources; even so, what contradiction would there be? Having thus described their origin, he now states the eightfold knowledge of diamonds: "Origin, qualities and defects, species, mines, movement of the fingers of the hand, price, the circular mark (*maṇḍalika*), and hardness—thus the knowledge of precious stones is eightfold."

In this context, although not stated in a single continuous flow, let the experts indeed understand each of those points individually as they are proclaimed verse by verse in the sections on examination. (27) *Maṇḍalī* means the assembly of jewel-examiners. Although the origin and other characteristics are mentioned in various separate verses, let them understand—let them know—all of them together at the time of examination. By this, the intended meaning is that the examination of diamonds should be conducted as if all the verses were unified, whether they are taken as a whole or individually.

Having established the ground, he now speaks of the *pave* (the sacrificial ladle): "The *pave* is to be known as fourfold, distinguished as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra. Furthermore, each of these is said to be threefold according to the division of male, female, and neuter (*napuṃsaka*). Among them, the twice-born (Brahmin) has a white luster like crystal; the King (Kṣatriya) is somewhat red; the Vaiśya is yellowish; and the twice-born (Brahmin) is dark-colored. Within that [category], this [last] is the male. (28)

That stone which is free from lines and spots, possesses eight facets, and has a clear luster is [the best]; however, that which is accompanied by six-sided figures, spots, and lines is described as [inferior]. Those that are without corners, flat, triangular in form, long, or irregular should respectively be assigned to women, men, and those called neuter (eunuchs). Having explained this: that which has a luster as white as crystal is a Brāhmaṇa; that which is slightly red is a Kṣatriya king; the rest is clear.

Now, he states that through the maintenance of the supreme *pavi* (vajra) and other practices, both Dharma and Artha are attained: "Whatever fruit a man obtains from the study of the Vedas, from the performance of a sacrifice, or even from ascetic penance—that he attains by maintaining the excellent body of the Vajra. [From the] Āyurvedīya-granthamālā, [verse] 166. (Note: The commentary clarifies that the term *pavi* refers to the *vajra*, which is here identified with the body; its maintenance leads to the attainment of spiritual and worldly goals.)

Furthermore, because he accepts the system of the four castes, let him by no means fail to embrace that supreme prosperity which is joined with the welfare resting upon the four varṇas. Now, he states that even a member of the Śūdra caste is more pure than a member of the foremost twice-born caste: "If a twice-born man is inferior even to a Śūdra due to being devoid of virtues, then this Śūdra, on account of his weightiness through virtues, deserves to stand higher even than a pure Brāhmaṇa."

Mental anguish, physical disease, serpents, fire, enemies, tigers, untimely death, and malevolent planets—these do not overcome him in whose house the pure *pavi* (sacred stone) resides. (31) Now, the defects of the *pavi* are taught: the "dot" (*bindu*), the "crow's foot" (*kākapada*), the "barley grain" (*yava*), "impurity" (*mala*), and the "line" (*rekhā*)—these five various defects of the *pavi* have been described here. Among them, the "dot" is equal to a [standard] dot.

Black and red are considered auspicious in that order; furthermore, they are distinguished by being elongated or circular. However, not every such mark is praised for the seeker, as it may be fruitless. For the seeker, a fruitless mark is one that does not bring about the acquisition of wealth and so forth. Not every dot (bindu) is auspicious. Now, he defines the "crow's foot" (kākapada): The "crow's foot" should be known by the examiner to be shaped like a crow’s claw. Furthermore, when this is situated in the *vī* [or *śrī*] line, it brings death to the wearer.

One should recognize the *yava* by its distinctions of red, yellow, white, and black; thus the *yava*-shaped gem is known to be fourfold. Among these, the white *yava* is indeed worthy of worship for the sake of the blade [of a sword], while the others are censured. (33) Now, he defines the *mala*: "The *mala* is explained by the wise as being threefold, according to whether it is situated at the edge, the corner, or the center of the gem. Furthermore, that [defect] causes the wearer fear of fire, tigers, and other such perils."

Now he defines the lines: "The one residing on the left side, the other situated there, the cutter, and the cut—these four lines are considered to have an upward course and a traversed path. (13) [From the] *Āyurvedaprakāśa*.

167. Now he speaks of their censure: "In that case, the others are auspicious; moreover, they grant great fortune. Even when [the moon] is in a circle, within the *bhadra* [division], or in a *lagna-kona*, the defects are ineffective. He states an exception to the defects mentioned here with the words "even when in a circle," etc. The meaning is that when the bridegroom is of such a nature, the defects are ineffective, i.e., fruitless.

Now, the virtuous praise these five qualities in the *pavī* (diamond) fit for the enjoyment of the gods: transparency, lightness, as well as the possession of eight facets, redness, and sharpness. In the best *pavīs*, transparency is like that of a mirror; lightness is like that of a chaff-seed; the possession of eight facets refers to having eight faces; and sharpness is the ability to cleave other gems—these are the five qualities.

Now, under the guise of a conclusion, he defines the *khani* (mines): "The *jāti* has been defined previously, and birth (*janman*) has also been mentioned; the *khani*, however, is eightfold. Among them, two prevail in each *yuga*; of these, the first is Kośala."

Immediately following that, Kāliṅga is mentioned; likewise Vaṅga, Mālava, Saurāṣṭra, Maṇipuṇḍraka, and then in the Kali age, Sopāra and Vajrākara (36). In the first age, the Kṛtayuga, there were Kośala (the country of Kośala) and the country of Kāliṅga; in the Tretāyuga, the country of Vaṅga and Mālava; in the Dvāpara, the country of Saurāṣṭra and Mount Maṇipuṇḍraka; but in the Kali age, the country of Sopāra and Vajrākara, which in the vernacular is called "Durāgaḍa."

Now, for the purpose of defining the fundamental units of knowledge (*mūlyajñāna*), he states the technical definitions of measures: four white mustard seeds (*sitasarṣapa*) make one *panasikā*; two of those make one grain of rice (*taṇḍula*); from those two [grains of rice] comes one barley grain (*yava*); and this cluster (*piṇḍa*) is somewhat broader than that.

The term *piṇḍa* (lump) and *gātra* (body) are two ways of expressing the same thing; having understood this designation and having weighed it with a scale, one should state its price. (37) 1. Regarding the word *piṇḍa*, Mahādeva states in his commentary on the *Rasapaddhati*: "The word *piṇḍa* denotes bulkiness; [one should say] 'this is thicker than a barley grain,' or 'it is slightly more [than that]'. 2. The reading in the *Rasapaddhati* is: "Having compared it with a measuring rod (*mānakadaṇḍa*), one should state whether it is of great, middling, or small value. (From the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, No. 168)

Regarding the statement that "its value must be declared after considering it," he says: "There is no uniform value for each region by which this [work] could be described by me in such a way; nevertheless, it is spoken here for the sake of ending the debate among the Trirāśikas. For instance, the *piṇḍa* (syllabic weight) is of three kinds: light, equal, and heavy. Among these, lightness is considered the best, equality is middling, and heaviness is said by the wise to be of the least value."

In three ways by lightness, in three ways by heaviness, and in six ways by commonality, the value is thus twelvefold; indeed, one should determine the price according to this gradual gradation. Having considered a lump [of gold] equal in size to a grain of rice, as broad as a barleycorn, and again having compared it with a forest [of such grains], one should then assign the price for four [such units].

If that diamond, endowed with the four qualities of gradual descent and so forth, is one *tandula* (grain) in size and as thick as a barley grain (*yava*), it obtains a price of forty [units]. Furthermore, for a lump whose measurement is equal to two barley grains, its price should be cited as five times four [twenty] *tandulas*. Again, if the lump consists of three barley grains, it would be thirty *tandulas*; for eight barley grains, sixteen; and for this diamond measured by *tandulas*, the price increases by two and two [respectively]. 41.

A gem that is like seven barley grains (*yava*) in size by nature receives, at first, a price increased by twenty-eight units per *māṇava*. If it is measured as being equal to one grain of rice (*taṇḍula*) in its mass, it is called a *vajra* or *vāritara*, and it obtains a maximum price of two thousand. If it is like a *sāvriya* in appearance, with a heavy weight for its size and a grain of rice that diminishes, this is the sequence for the decrease in the price of such a gem.

Having thus investigated by means of the power of reasoning, one should determine the value of the four [qualities] of the jewel; just as when there is no flaw in a diamond (*vajravarma*), one might consider its excellence to be complete.
