Thus ends the chapter on pearls. Now follows the description of diamonds. A diamond that is clear, sharp-edged, and possesses the brilliance of a blue lotus is said to be the best. It destroys all diseases and grants victory. One should wear a diamond that is heavy, well-proportioned, and free from flaws, for it bestows sovereignty and removes all calamities. However, one should avoid those that are dull, cracked, or have a yellowish tint, as they bring ill fortune. Thus ends the chapter on diamonds. Now follows the description of rubies. A ruby that is deep red like the rising sun, without spots, and possesses a brilliant luster is most auspicious. It bestows wealth, fame, and long life. One should wear a ruby that is hard, smooth, and well-rounded. Those that are pale, spotted, or have a black center should be avoided. Thus ends the chapter on rubies. Now follows the description of emeralds. An emerald that is green like a parrot’s wing or a fresh sprout, and is transparent and flawless, is highly praised. It pacifies all planetary afflictions and bestows peace. One should wear an emerald that is heavy and has a uniform color. Those that are pale, cracked, or have a yellowish tinge should be rejected. Thus ends the chapter on emeralds. Now follows the description of sapphires. A sapphire that is deep blue like the throat of a peacock or the sky at twilight, and is hard and lustrous, is most excellent. It protects against poison and evil spirits. One should wear a sapphire that is pure and without internal flaws. Those that are dull, spotted, or have a white streak should be avoided. Thus ends the chapter on sapphires. Now follows the description of coral. Coral that is bright red like the Bimba fruit or the rising sun, and is smooth and without pits, is auspicious. It increases vitality and wards off evil influences. One should wear coral that is heavy and has a consistent color. Those that are pale, porous, or have a black spot should be rejected. Thus ends the chapter on coral. Now follows the description of pearls again. A pearl that is round, white, and smooth, and which does not lose its luster even when rubbed, is the best. It bestows health and prosperity. One should wear a pearl that is heavy and has a brilliant glow. Those that are flat, rough, or have a dark core should be avoided. Thus ends the chapter on pearls. Now follows the description of gold. Gold that is soft, malleable, and shines like fire is the most excellent. It bestows longevity and removes all sins. One should wear gold that is pure and free from alloys. That which is brittle, dark, or smells of sulfur should be rejected. Thus ends the chapter on gold. Now follows the description of silver. Silver that is white, soft, and malleable is auspicious. It bestows purity and removes poverty. One should wear silver that is bright and free from stains. That which is dull, porous, or has a black tint should be avoided. Thus ends the chapter on silver. Now follows the description of copper. Copper that is red like the Bandhujīva flower and is malleable is best. It bestows strength and wards off evil eyes. One should wear copper that is pure and has a bright luster. That which is black, brittle, or smells of sulfur should be rejected. Thus ends the chapter on copper. Now follows the description of iron. Iron that is black, hard, and capable of cutting is the best. It bestows power and destroys enemies. One should wear iron that is tempered and free from rust. That which is brittle, porous, or has a yellowish tint should be avoided. Thus ends the chapter on iron. Now follows the description of gems in general. Gems that are heavy, hard, and possess a brilliant luster are auspicious. They bestow sovereignty and remove all obstacles. One should wear gems that are pure and have been consecrated with mantras. Those that are dull, cracked, or have a dark core should be rejected. Thus ends the chapter on gems. Now follows the description of the testing of gems. A gem should be tested by its weight, its luster, its hardness, and its clarity. One who knows these qualities will never be deceived. Thus ends the chapter on the testing of gems. Now follows the description of the wearing of gems. Gems should be worn according to one's birth star and the specific planetary influence. Worn properly, they grant success; worn improperly, they cause harm. Thus ends the chapter on the wearing of gems. Now follows the description of the purification of gems. Gems should be purified by rubbing them with ashes, acids, or oils, depending on their nature. Once purified, they shine with renewed brilliance. Thus ends the chapter on the purification of gems. Now follows the description of the benefits of wearing gems. By wearing a pure gem, one gains wisdom, health, and wealth. It protects the wearer from all dangers and ensures a long life. Thus ends the chapter on the benefits of wearing gems. Now follows the description of the omens regarding gems. If a gem becomes cloudy or loses its luster, it portends some misfortune. One should perform rituals of propitiation or replace the gem. Thus ends the chapter on omens regarding gems. Now follows the description of the storage of gems. Gems should be stored in a clean, dry place, protected from dust and moisture. They should be wrapped in silk or kept in a box made of precious metal. Thus ends the chapter on the storage of gems. Now follows the description of the value of gems. The value of a gem depends on its size, its weight, its color, and its purity. A gem that is large, heavy, and perfectly colored is of the highest value. Thus ends the chapter on the value of gems. Now follows the description of the history of gems. Gems were first discovered in the ocean by the gods and demons during their churning. Since then, they have been distributed throughout the world. Thus ends the chapter on the history of gems. Now follows the description of the classification of gems. Gems are classified into nine types: diamond, ruby, emerald, sapphire, pearl, coral, topaz, lapis lazuli, and cat’s eye. Each has its own specific properties and uses. Thus ends the chapter on the classification of gems. Now follows the description of the mantras for gems. For each type of gem, there is a specific mantra to be recited during its consecration. These mantras empower the gem and enhance its protective qualities. Thus ends the chapter on the mantras for gems. Now follows the description of the yantras for gems. A yantra inscribed on a gem multiplies its power tenfold. It should be drawn according to the rules of sacred geometry and charged with energy. Thus ends the chapter on the yantras for gems. Now follows the description of the gems of the celestial beings. The gods possess gems of incomparable brilliance, such as the Cintāmaṇi and the Kaustubha. These are beyond the reach of mortals. Thus ends the chapter on the gems of the celestial beings. Now follows the description of the gems of the nāgas. The nāgas possess gems that grant invisibility and protection from poison. These are known as the Nāga-maṇis. Thus ends the chapter on the gems of the nāgas. Now follows the description of the gems of the yakṣas. The yakṣas possess gems that fulfill all desires and grant wealth. These are known as the Yakṣa-maṇis. Thus ends the chapter on the gems of the yakṣas. Now follows the description of the gems of the rākṣasas. The rākṣasas possess gems that grant the power of flight and invisibility. These are known as the Rākṣasa-maṇis. Thus ends the chapter on the gems of the rākṣasas. Now follows the description of the gems of the gandharvas. The gandharvas possess gems that grant the power of music and enchantment. These are known as the Gandharva-maṇis. Thus ends the chapter on the gems of the gandharvas. Now follows the description of the gems of the kinnaras. The kinnaras possess gems that grant the power of song and beauty. These are known as the Kinnara-maṇis. Thus ends the chapter on the gems of the kinnaras. Now follows the description of the gems of the siddhas. The siddhas possess gems that grant the eight supernatural powers (aṣṭasiddhis). These are known as the

That which remains unaltered even when rubbed with rice husks is considered a genuine pearl (muktika). The pearl is very sweet, cooling, a pacifier of eye diseases, and a destroyer of poison. It eliminates the aggravation of *rājayakṣman* (consumption), and increases the nourishment of diminished semen, strength, and vitality. It destroys phlegm (*kapha*), bile (*pitta*), and wasting (*kṣaya*), and removes cough, asthma, and weak digestion. It is considered to bestow nourishment, to be aphrodisiac, life-prolonging, and a remedy for burning sensations. Now, [the section on] ruby (*māṇikya*) and *padmarāga*.

The ruby (māṇikya) is sweet, glossy, and a destroyer of wind and bile; for those with knowledge of the application of gems, it is the supreme elixir (rasāyana). (97) A ruby produced in that region which is glossy, fashioned from beautiful limbs, radiant, clear, and well-colored brings auspiciousness through its wearing. (98) That ruby which is lusterless, gritty, rough, deficient in color, or deformed should not be worn; it brings harm and must be rejected. (99)

— 1 ‘Kṛṣṇatā’ (blackness), Ga. 178. Āyurvedīyagranthamālā. [Chapter] A ruby (*māṇikya*) that has the luster of a lotus petal, is transparent, glossy, large, clear, circular or oblong, and symmetrical in its parts is auspicious in eight ways. (100) Ruby stimulates digestion, is aphrodisiac, and removes the pain caused by *kapha* and *vāta*. It wards off ghosts and *vetālas*, destroys sins, and cures diseases born of past actions (*karmaja*). (101) Now, regarding emerald (*garutmat*): Emerald indeed destroys poison, is cooling, and sweet in taste.

It cures acidity, stimulates the appetite, provides nourishment, and destroys evil spirits. A body that is clear, heavy, well-proportioned, glossy, and possesses a deep luster is considered auspicious; likewise, emerald (marakata) is deemed auspicious when it is unblemished, multicolored, and radiant. Conversely, that which is gravelly, dry, dirty, light, lacking luster, and mottled is inferior.

Even an immortal would not consume emerald that is mixed with base substances or is disfigured. (104) That which is constantly endowed with the qualities of moss, peacock feathers, the *śāṅgalaharika* grass, crow’s wings, fireflies, the young *kaurava* flower, and the *śairīṣa* flower—such is the eightfold natural emerald (*gārutmata*) which, when heated by the sun’s rays, radiates all around. (105) Now, its medicinal action (*aiṅkarya*): it is beneficial for the eyes, sour in taste, and destroys phlegm and wind.

That which pacifies disorders such as *gulma* and other ailments, and is born of the earth, brings auspiciousness. It should be known by three types of luster: one with the soft brilliance of a *vepalāśa* leaf, another with the hue of the gleaming eyes of a cat, and the third with a tawny complexion. That *vaiḍūrya* which possesses weight at night, is glossy, free from defects, transparent, and split open, is declared by the wise to be excellent. However, that which is lusterless, contains earth or stone within, is light, and is rough, is considered inferior.

A messenger should discard a lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*) that is accompanied by fear, flattened, or black. (108) Lapis lazuli that has a dark-white luster, is even, clear, heavy, and transparent, and is encased within a whirling, beautiful upper garment, is declared auspicious. (109) When a stone, being itself clear and polished, clearly displays its own reflection upon the surface of a touchstone, such lapis lazuli is called genuine (*jātya*). (110)

Vaiḍūrya destroys *raktapitta* (bile-blood disorders), increases progeny, longevity, and strength, cures diseases dominated by *pitta*, and is both digestive (*dīpana*) and aphrodisiac (*vṛṣya*). Now, regarding *gomeda*: Gomeda that is well-clear like the luster of cow’s urine, unctuous, transparent, even, heavy, free of flaws, smooth, and radiant is auspicious; it is of eight types. Gomeda is sour and hot; it conquers disorders arising from the provocation of *vāta*. It is digestive, promotes digestion, and when worn, it destroys sins.

When placed in a vessel, that *gomeda* gem which causes milk to blaze like cow’s urine while retaining its natural luster is known by the wise as being of noble birth (*jātya*). (114) *Gomeda* destroys phlegm and bile, cures consumption and anemia, stimulates digestion, promotes maturation, improves appetite, is beneficial for the skin, and awakens the intellect. (115) *Lomeda* that is lusterless, light, dry, marked with spots, flattened, covered with layers, devoid of brilliance, or resembling yellow glass does not bring auspicious results. (116) Now, the sapphire (*indranīla*).

Uniform in luster, heavy, glossy, transparent, and compact in form; soft, yielding when rubbed, and shining with light—such is the excellent sevenfold blue sapphire (nīla). As praised by Nīla, it removes asthma and cough, is aphrodisiac, destroys the three *doṣas*, and is a great digestive stimulant. It destroys irregular fevers, difficulties in speech, and sins. Blue sapphire is bitter, excellent, and dispels phlegm, bile, and wind. He who wears it becomes like Śauri (Viṣṇu) and a bestower of auspiciousness. It is not brittle, pure, resonant when struck, smooth, and firm.

One who is endowed with auspicious marks is as difficult to find as a blade of grass grasped by the wind. (120) [From the] *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter 180: White, red, yellow, and black—these are said to be the colors [of the luster] in the blue stone respectively. Its wearing also brings results like those of a diamond, provided it is established as belonging to the [appropriate] caste, such as the Brāhmaṇa and others. (121) That vessel which is filled with milk made beautiful by the flow of moonlight and quickly colors [the stone], that is called a genuine blue sapphire (*nīla*). (122) Now, the topaz (*puṣparāga*).

A pure topaz that possesses a luster, is yellow, heavy, has beautiful limbs, and is smooth, clean, perfectly round, and very cool; which destroys decay and nourishes fame, great valor, happiness, long life, and wealth—[that is the best]. (123) O Yakṣa, a topaz that is marred by black spots, white or soiled, light, lusterless, and resembling sugar or charcoal is full of defects. (124) That which, when rubbed on the touchstone, displays its own color even more intensely, is considered excellent.

Indeed, this is called *puṣparāga* (topaz) by experts when it is of high quality. The *puṣparāga* is heavy, glossy, clear, large, even, soft, resembling the hue of the *karṇikāra* flower, smooth, and auspicious; thus it is of eight kinds. *Puṣparāga* removes poison, vomiting, phlegm, wind, and sluggish digestion; it pacifies skin diseases, hemorrhoids, and burning sensations, and is digestive, light, and a promoter of digestion.

Now, the appropriate characteristics for all [gems] are as follows: the sapphire (*indranīla*) should be dark blue; the emerald (*gārutmata*) should have an extremely smooth surface and a dark luster, though it may be highly brilliant; the sun-gem (*mihiramaṇi*) should glow when heated by the sun and emit sparks of fire; the moon-gem (*śaśimaṇi*) should exude water upon contact with the moon or other such objects; the topaz (*puṣparāga*) resembles a flower; and the precious diamond (*śrīvajra*), when struck by a hammer, should sink into a lump of iron.

That which has the luster of a *viḍālīkṣaṇa* (cat's eye) is called *vaiḍūrya*; the *gomedaka* gem is said to have the appearance of cow’s urine; they call the *padmarāga* (ruby) like a smokeless, blazing fire. Pearls are born from oyster shells, coral from the sea, and these are world-renowned. But they say the *rājāvarta* arises from a portion of the earth that is yellowish-red, soft, and fragrant. (Āyurvedaprakāśa, 181) Now, the five gems: topaz (*puṣparāga*), sapphire (*mahānīla*), ruby (*padmarāga*), and *vajra* (diamond).

The emerald (marakata) is also proclaimed; these are the five auspicious and excellent gems. Now, as for the jewels: vaikrānta, sūryakānta, diamond (hīraka), pearl (mauktika), moonstone (candrakānta), and rājāvarta as the seventh—these, along with garuḍodāraka, are to be known as the jewels. These include those previously mentioned. Now, regarding the origin of the jewels other than those [made of] mercury (vaṅga): gomedaka, tārkṣya, yajñaja, devejya, maṇi, indu, taraṇikānta, and others.

The various types of crystal (*sphaṭika*) should be understood by those who are discerning as being enriched with diverse colors and qualities. [Vāyaja, Vaiḍūrya, Devejya, Puṣparāga, and the rest are] clear. Now, regarding *sphaṭika*: it is a white stone, a stainless gem, a pure stone, transparent, a clear gem, a spotless jewel, a flawless gem, and beloved by fire; thus it is ninefold. (133) Crystal possesses balanced potency (*vīrya*); it cures the afflictions of bile, burning sensations, and consumption. A rosary made from it bestows ten-million-fold fruit upon one who recites mantras. (134)

That which, when broken, possesses the luster of a drop of water; which is most pure, stainless, pleasing to the eye and heart, glossy, clear within, sweet, and exceedingly cool; which removes bile, burning sensations, and blood disorders; and which, even when ground by stones and shattered, never abandons its own transparency—knowing such a source to be obtainable there, one attains various auspicious and wondrous Śiva-pearls. Now, it is called *sūryakānta*, *tapanamaṇi*, *tapana*, *ravikānta*, *dīptopala*, *agnigarbha*, *jvalana*, *arkopala*, and *vasunāman*.

136 || The *ravikānta* (sun-stone) is hot, pure, and an elixir (*rasāyana*); it removes wind and phlegm (*vāta-śleṣman*), promotes intelligence, and grants satisfaction to the Sun through worship. 137 || That which is pure, unctuous, free from flaws, and devoid of husks, and which attains extreme brilliance when rubbed on the edge, is [the sun-stone]. [From the] Āyurvedīyagranthamālā. [Chapter: That which arises from fire produced by the contact of the sun's rays is called *sūryakānta*. 138 || *Indukānta*, *candrakānta*, *candrāma*, and *candrajopala* [are synonyms for the moon-stone].

The moonstone (*candrakānta*) is of seven kinds: *śītātman*, *candrikādrāva*, and *śaśikānta*. It is cool, glossy, and removes bile, blood, and heat. It bestows auspiciousness and prosperity, is transparent, and destroys the inauspiciousness caused by the planets. That which is glossy, cool, yellow, and possesses transparency within its core like that of sages, and which oozes upon contact with the rays of the moon, is the noble gem known as *candrakānta*. It is also called *rājāvarta*, *nṛpāvarta*, and *rājanyāvartaka*.

The *āvatemaṇi* is called *āvarta*; this is known by the name *śara*. *Rājāvarta* is pungent, unctuous, cooling, and destroys *pitta*. When employed in ornaments, it brings good fortune to men. They say that the noble *rājāvarta* gem is black, heavy, smooth, pure, and highly lustrous; it is gentle and resembles the throat of a peacock. *Peroja*, *haritāśma*, *bhasāṅga*, and *harita* are of two kinds.

Pīroja is astringent, sweet, digestive, and laxative (145). It quickly destroys all poisons—whether derived from stationary or moving sources, or even those produced by combination—as well as diseases arising from the fundamental humors (doṣas) such as vāta and the rest (146). Thus it is said. Now follows the purification and killing of all gems; and it is stated: "These various gems must be purified with great care. If unpurified, they do not produce their beneficial qualities, but rather spread diseases" (147). [13] *Āyurvedaprakāśa*.

Puṣparāga [topaz] is purified by being suspended in a mixture of horse-gram decoction and rice-water; nīla [sapphire] by indigo juice; gomeda by the waters of *rocanā* (yellow pigment); and vaiḍūrya [cat's eye] by the waters of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). When heated in these solutions while suspended in a crucible on a swing (*dolā*), they are quickly purified. Other gems, excluding the *vana* [emerald], are indeed killed by being subjected to eight layers of a paste made from *śilā* (realgar), *tālaka* (orpiment), and *gandhaka* (sulphur) ground with the juice of *lakucha*. This concludes the process for reducing all [gems] to ash.

In this regard, there is a certain distinction: if gems and the like are unavailable, one should take a secondary gem (uparatna) for them; and in the absence of pearls, one should employ a pearl-oyster shell. Here, the venerable teachers [state]: "A wise person should not destroy the nine gems, such as diamonds and others; for they possess great value, and by destroying them, one incurs the sin of killing a cow. (152-153)

If so, why did the sages speak of the act of killing? It is for the purpose of removing the body [of the disease], and there exists a further seed of instruction received from others, as follows: "When a purification of clothes and such is being performed, the small fragments that fall from the limbs—one who is wise should kill them. For those which are born from that very source, being of the same nature and possessing good characteristics, yet having little value—there is no sin in this world in their killing."

Thus [ends verse] 155. Furthermore: "Just as the qualities of gems [are lost] when they have perished, so it is with those [other stones]; they are slightly inferior to them. This distinction has been illustrated. [Verse] 156. Now, regarding the origin, names, qualities, purification, and calcination of *vaikrānta*, which is among the secondary gems (*uparatna*): When the great Daitya known as Mahiṣāsura was slain by the Goddess, wherever indeed the drops of blood extracted from his body fell during the battle upon the southern and northern slopes of the Vindhya mountain, [there this gem arose]. [Verse] 157.

Those which have the form of diamonds are born as those renowned as *vaikrānta*. (158) In the *Gaurīmata*, however, it is said: "Those irregular diamond fragments that bear the name *vaikrānta*—their varieties, methods of purification, and properties are like those of the diamond (*vajra*). (159) Furthermore, O Bhairava, having worshipped Gaṇanātha preceded by an offering (*bali*), the wise should then collect *vaikrānta* at an auspicious moment. (160)

Vaikrānta is of various types according to distinctions such as white, yellow, and so forth; it is considered auspicious for producing gold, silver, and other metals, each possessing its own characteristic color. That vaikrānta which is black in color, hexagonal or octagonal, lustrous, heavy, and pure, bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis). Vaikrānta possesses qualities similar to diamond (vajra) and is held to strengthen the body and the blood; it is an antidote to mercury-poisoning and destroys fever, leprosy, and consumption.

In other contexts as well, vaikrānta destroys the three doṣas, possesses the six tastes, and provides firmness to the body; it cures anemia, abdominal enlargement, fever, asthma, cough, consumption, and urinary disorders. (164) If impure, both vajra and vaikrānta cause leucoderma, a burning sensation, and continuous pain; they produce anemia and side-pain, but once purified, they remove these ailments. (165) For purification and killing, vaikrānta is to be processed like vajra: it should be heated and sprinkled with horse-urine. Having attained death like vajra, it should be employed in place of vajra. (166)

Vaikrānta is purified by being washed in a decoction of *kulitha* (horse gram). It is killed by eight *puṭas* when combined with the juice of *gandhanimbūka*. [167] Thus ends the section on Vaikrānta from the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*. In every variety, however, when ground using the method of sublimation (*capātana-yoga*) and made into pills, Vaikrānta situated in an ornament will release its impurity after a period of one *ghaṭikā*. [168] Thus ends the section on the purification of Vaikrānta.

Now, another method: One *pala* of *vaikrānta* and one *karṣa* of *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax) should be soaked for a day in the milky sap of the *arka* plant and for a day in the juice of *śigru*. One should add one *pratīkarṣa* each of *guñjā*, oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), and *vīnā*. Having formed a pill with this, one should heat it strongly in a crucible; the essence (*satva*) produced from *vaikrānta* will become like a jasmine flower or the moon. Thus ends the section on *vaikrānta-satva*.

The method for purifying and processing other stones, as well as their qualities, is as follows: gems, precious stones, *cakṣuṣya* stones, and corals destroy planets, misfortune, poison, evil spirits, sins, and afflictions. When consumed, they indeed destroy consumption, jaundice, urinary disorders (*prameha*), hemorrhoids, cough, asthma, fistula-in-ano, fever, erysipelas, leprosy, pain, gravel, and various diseases; they bestow merit and fame, and greatly increase the virtues of men. Now, for the sake of propitiating the nine planets, one should wear a ring set with the nine gems.

Of that [earth], the eastern direction belongs to the diamond (*vajra*); the south-eastern to the ruby (*māṇikya*); the southern direction to the emerald (*vaidūrya*); the south-western to the *gomeda*; the western to the sapphire (*nīlāśman*); the north-western to the *vaidūrya* (cat's-eye); the northern direction to the coral (*puṣpa*); and the remaining direction, the north-east, belongs to the emerald (*marakata*). 173.

*Kuliśa* is diamond (*vajra*); *vīprabhava* is coral (*pravāla*); *nīlāśu* is sapphire (*indranīla*); *vid* is lapis lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*); *puṣpa* is topaz (*puṣparāga*); *harinmaṇi* is emerald; *garuḍodbhāra* is chrysoberyl (*gārutmat*). [This is from the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, chapter on the *Aiśānī* [direction], regarding the remaining *māṇikya* [ruby]; the remaining direction is the center; the meaning is that one should place [the gems] upon the pericarp. Now, for one who is unable [to perform rituals], he states the wearing and giving [of gems] as a counter-measure against the malevolence of the planets: "Ruby for the Sun, emerald for Mars, chrysoberyl for Jupiter, topaz for Venus, gomedaka for Saturn, coral for Mercury, and pearl for the Moon."

They say that for the Sun, for Rāhu (Tamas), for Mars (Avanīmūnu), for Saturn (Mandagati), for Venus (Kavi), and for Jupiter (Kuliśaketu), the cat’s-eye gem (vidūraka) is prescribed for giving or wearing; this is to be done as appropriate when these planets are in a state of adversity. (Note: *Dhūmaṇi* is a variant for *dhūmaketu*, referring to the comet-like Rāhu; *kuliśaketu* refers to Jupiter, whose banner bears a thunderbolt.)

Now he describes the liquefaction (*druti*) of pearls and other gems as well: "One should soak pearls for seven days in the acid of *vetasa* (cane). Then, having placed them inside a *jambīra* fruit, one should bury it in a heap of grain. By means of *puṭapāka* (sealed-pot cooking), that powder liquefies like water. O Dear One, this king of formulations effects the liquefaction of gems. Thus ends the liquefaction of pearls and other gems. Now, regarding the liquefaction of *saurāṣṭrī* (borax): "One should soak white and black *saurāṣṭrī* with cow-dung."

One should carefully heat it one hundred times while joined with the five friends (*mitrapañcaka*) in a crucible-furnace (*koṣṭhayantre*). Then, regarding the essence of *sasyaka*: powdered *sasyaka* should be infused for one day with rabbit blood or with female urine, or else for one watch (*yāma*). One should add a quarter part of that [infusion] along with *niśā* (turmeric). Then, having formed a ball (*golaka*) with *marica* and *karañja* oil, it should be placed in a blind crucible (*andhamūṣā*) and heated with a strong fire for half a *ghaṭikā*.

It emits a beautiful sound resembling that of the *indragopaka* insect. Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*, composed by the venerable Mādhava, a teacher and ornament of the Sārasvata lineage born in the region of Surāṣṭra. [Chapter 13]. [Note: 1. 'jhamake ga' refers to a variant reading]. Chapter 14.

*Āyurvedaprakāśa*, Chapter Fourteen Now, I shall explain this chapter concerning the characteristics, species, qualities, consumption, and avoidance of poisons (*viṣa*) and minor poisons (*upaviṣa*). First, the origin of poison: Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim where the great poison originated, its various types, O lady of excellent hips, and their locations in detail. (1) O fair-faced one, the gods, Daityas, serpents, Siddhas, Apsaras, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and Kinnaras all gathered together. (2)

On one side was King Bali, and likewise on the other side were Brahmā and the other gods. Having made Mount Mandara the churning stick and encircled it with the King of Serpents, O beautiful goddess, the churning of the Ocean of Milk was commenced there. Thereafter, excellent jewels such as the nectar emerged from it. Then, O Goddess, due to the excessive churning and the force of the blows from Mount Mandara, as well as from the exhaustion of the King of Serpents, a flame of poison issued forth. Then that most terrible flame sank into the Ocean of Milk.

(Likewise, the great poison Kālakūṭa arose right there—resembling the fire of universal dissolution, fierce like the wrathful God of Death. Seeing that, all the gods and the exceedingly powerful Dānavas immediately became dejected in countenance and came into my presence. Then, being entreated by them, I drank that supreme poison. Thereafter, that poison remained in its original form: in some places as leaves, and in others as clay.

The characteristics of these [poisons] are described in some places according to their bulbous form (*kanda-rūpa*). Poison is known by the names *viṣa*, *garala*, *veḍa*, and *kālakūṭa*. Wise men should know that there are eighteen types of poison born from bulbs (*kandabhava*). Among them, eight are of the mild variety (*saumya-bheda*); they kill a human being upon ingestion. Ten varieties are killers through touch or even by smelling. [From the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter 188: As for example: *saktuka*, *mustaka*, *kauma*, *dārvāka*, and likewise *sārṣapa*.

*Saikata*, *vatsanābha*, and likewise *śvetā-jī*—one should collect these eight poisons for medicinal purposes. Indeed, when practiced according to the prescribed method, they remove old age and disease. (11–12) *Lakṣaṇāna* has variegated spots and resembles the bulb of a blue lotus; when well-ground, it becomes like flour. One should know that as *saktuka*; it has a long-lasting effect and is extremely potent. (13) *Iskhavega* is a disease-causer; *mustaka* is shaped like *mustaka* grass. *Karma* has the shape of a tortoise, while *dārvaka* indeed has the shape of a hooded serpent.

14–17 || The *sārṣapa* (mustard) bulb, which removes fever, is found on the *romi* plant and is accompanied by mustard-like grains; it is possessed of coarse and fine particles, and its hairs are white and yellow. This bulb, which destroys all diseases beginning with fever, is called *saikata*. That bulb which is shaped like a cow’s teat, neither long nor exceeding five finger-breadths in size, and not thicker than a cow’s teat, is the two-fold *vatsanābha* (vatsanāga). It is a quick-acting, light, and easily discarded substance; it may be white or black, otherwise being different. It is to be employed for the removal of diseases, for *jāraṇā*, and for *rasāyana*.

The *jhāṅgī* plant is shaped like a cow’s horn; it is white on the outside and [dark] within. (18) One should employ these—saktuka and the others—in cases of *vātarakta* involving all three *doṣas*, as well as in cases of delusion (*moha*), insanity (*unmāda*), epilepsy (*apasmṛti*), and skin diseases (*kuṣṭha*). (19) Regarding *vātarakta*, the essential meaning is that it may be a disease where *vāta* is predominant, where blood (*rakta*) is predominant, or where both are predominant. Now, the things to be avoided: *kālakūṭa*, *meṣī*, *dardūraka*, *hālāhala*, *karkoṭa*, *granthi*, and *haridraka*. (20)

1. [The term] *dīrgharoga* is found in manuscript *ga*. 2. [The term] *sarṣapābhakaṇākṛti* is found in manuscript *ga*. 14] Regarding the manifestation of the lifespan: "The *raktī*, *kesara*, and *yamadaṃṣṭrā*—these ten poisons should be avoided by the wise in medicinal formulations according to their true nature. 21. "In the battle between the gods and the asuras, those slain by the gods were adorned with garlands of blood; from the blood of the Daitya, a tree resembling the *aśvattha* grew. 22. The resinous exudation (*niryāsa*) of this [tree] is proclaimed by the sages to be *kālakūṭa*."

It is found in Sohaicchatra, Śṛṅgavera, Koṅkaṇa, and Malaya. (23) Śṛṅgavera is a particular mountain. That which is thick, rough, very hard, and has a luster like split collyrium is declared to be the bulbous root known as the great poison Kālakūṭa. (24) Another characteristic: that bulbous root which is round, dry, and like a *jambīra* fruit—one should know that to be Kālakūṭa, which causes death by the mere smell. (25) A bulbous root shaped like a ram’s horn is called *meṣī*.

The bulbous root that has the appearance of a leprosy sore is called *dadru*. (26) The cluster (*guccha*) which has fruits resembling cow’s udders and leaves like palm fronds, by whose brilliance nearby trees and other objects are scorched—(27) this should be known as *hālāhala*. It grows in Kiṣkindhā on the Himalayas, as well as on the shores of the southern ocean and in the region of Koṅkaṇa. (28) That which is blue within and white without is declared to be *hālāhala*. *Karkoṭa* is the *karkoṭāma*; it is hard at the tip but soft in the middle. (29)

That tuber (kanda) is like a turmeric knot; it is black and extremely terrifying. It is rounded at the root and tip, elongated, and has a yellow interior. Rich in *kathaṅkā* (a type of resin), with smooth surfaces, that tuber is indeed *hāridra*. When placed on the forehead or the tip of the nose, blood flows from the nostrils. [From the] *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter 190: The tuber is small, and its poison is called *navadraktī*.

When dry, it possesses filaments; in its center, they know that to be the *kesara*. Shaped like a dog’s fang, it is called *yamadaṃṣṭra*. These ten are employed in elixirs (*rasāyana*), in alchemy (*dhātuvāda*), and in the application of poisons (*viṣavāda*) here and there, but not in medicinal elixirs. Now, nine varieties have been mentioned by some, as follows: *vatsanābha*, *sahāridra*, *saktuka*, *pradīpana*, *saurāṣṭrika*, *śṛṅgika*, and likewise *kālakūṭa*.

Hālāhala, Brahmaputra—these are the nine varieties of poison. They have leaves like those of the *palāśa* tree and fruits resembling *tīkṣṇa*. Its bulb is thick, and its power is said to be great. That which has leaves like the *sinduvāra* and a shape like *vatsanābha* is described as such; because there is no growth of the tree near it, it is called *vasanābha*. That which is red in color, white, and has the brilliance of fire, causing a great burning sensation upon smelling, is declared to be *pradīpana*.

That which is tawny in color and likewise possesses a core (sāraka) should be known as the son of Brahmā; it is born on the Malaya mountain. The remaining [qualities] have already been mentioned previously.

Now, their places of origin are as follows: Vatsanābha is produced on the Parvataka mountain; Hāridra in the thickets of Haridrā; Saktuka in the region of the mountains; Pradīpana in the Samakakṣa regions; Saurāṣṭrika in the country of Surāṣṭra; Phuṅgika in the thickets of the Kapi rivers; Kālakūṭa in Ahicchatra and other such places; Hālāhala in Kiṣkindhā and other such places; and Brahmaputra in the thickets of that mountain region named Brahma.

Now, their colors are as follows: the Brāhmaṇa is white (pāṇḍu), the Kṣatriya is red-colored, the Vaiśya has a yellow luster, and the Śūdra is black-colored and censured. [14] In the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*: the Brāhmaṇa is given for disease, the Kṣatriya for consuming poison, the Vaiśya for all ailments, and the Śūdra for one bitten by a snake. Now, the qualities of poison: poison is a rejuvenator (*rasāyana*), strengthening, and it removes disorders of wind (*vāta*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).

It is pungent, bitter, and astringent; it causes exhilaration and bestows happiness. It is pervasive (vyavāyi), dispels cold, is heating, and destroys skin diseases (kuṣṭha), hemorrhagic disorders (vātāsra), sluggish digestion (agnimāndya), dyspnea, cough, splenic enlargement, abdominal dropsy, fistula-in-ano, abdominal tumors (gulma), anemia, ulcers, and consumption when consumed according to the prescribed method. Elsewhere also, poison is said to be life-taking, pervasive (vyavāyi), and diffusive (vikāśi); it is fiery (āgneya), removes wind and phlegm, is systemically distributed through combination (yogavāhi), and produces great intoxication. That very same [substance], however, when properly prepared with appropriate methods, becomes life-giving and an elixir (rasāyana).

It is wholesome for one who eats properly, pacifies the three *doṣas*, is nourishing, and increases vitality (*vīrya*). It is pervasive (*vyavāyi*), having the nature of reaching the entire body and undergoing digestion; it is expansive (*vikāśi*), having the nature of first drying up the vital essence (*ojas*) and then loosening the binding of the joints; it is fiery (*āgneya*), causing great hunger; it is "conveying by association" (*yogavāhi*), meaning it takes on the qualities of whatever it is combined with; it brings about intoxication (*mada*) and, through an excess of the quality of *tamas*, destroys the intellect. Now, regarding the purification of poison: those evil qualities that reside in the poison shall be diminished once it has been purified.

Therefore, in the administration of poisons, the physician should employ [the substance] after it has been purified. Just as one would extract [a fruit] when its ripening is complete—fresh, unctuous, dense, heavy, not stripped of its skin, and not dried out by wind or other elements—one should treat it with anti-venomous agents such as peacock feathers and the like. Having made portions of the poison as large as chickpeas, one should place them in a vessel and pour fresh cow’s urine over them every day. [From the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, verse 192.]

One should dry it for three days and then place it in intense sunlight; thereafter, one should employ that poison in medicinal applications according to the prescribed dosage. This purification is appropriate during the summer season because of the presence of intense heat. One should wear the carefully purified poison on a cloth smeared with red mustard oil, for otherwise its potency is lost. Now, in the absence of intense sunlight, there is another method of purification: having made the poison into pieces as thick as chickpeas, one should steam them.

That poison attains purification in cow’s milk within five *ghaṭikās*. For any poison or secondary poison (*upaviṣa*) for which no specific purification has been prescribed, one should perform a sweating process (*khedana*) in cow’s milk to effect its purification. In the *Yogataraṅgiṇī*: "Having cut the poison into small pieces, one should tie it with a piece of cloth, place it in the midst of cow urine, and keep it in the sun for three days. Fresh cow urine should be provided daily by the wise. (50–52)

After three days have passed, one should extract it, dry it gently, and grind it finely. Thus purified, the poison becomes fit for medicinal use and conquers diseases. (53) Now follows another method: having cut the poison into pieces and bound it in cloth, one should purify it by suspending it on a swing (*dolā*) and boiling it in goat’s milk for one *yāma*. (54) In the absence of goat’s milk, one should purify it with cow’s milk. Thus freed from defects, the poison may be employed in medicinal formulations. (55)

Now, another method: having placed the poison-knot (*viṣagranthi*) in a buffalo hide and sealed it firmly, one should cook it for one *yāma* in a fire of dried cow dung; the poison, when purified by a cloth-strainer, becomes pure. Thus ends the purification of poison. (A = 14) In the *Āyurvedaprakāśa*: That poison, ground together with *ṭaṅkaṇa* (borax), is said to be "dead" (*mṛta*); one may employ it in all diseases, and it does not cause any adverse reaction. (57) Another opinion: [It should be prepared] with an equal amount of *śṛṅga* (horn) and double the amount of *upaṇa* (salt).

Poison that has been processed and purified becomes entirely non-toxic. Thus ends the section on the preparation and the lethal application of poison. Now, regarding the therapeutic use of poison: those diseases which are difficult to cure with various medicinal juices do not persist here; they are swiftly destroyed when poison is administered, especially those arising from wind (vāta) and phlegm (kapha). One should not administer it during the autumn, summer, spring, or the rainy seasons; however, during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, one may administer it according to the prescribed rite and dosage. Within four months, it removes diseases such as leprosy (kuṣṭha), spider-bites (lūtā), and others.

Poison should not be administered to one who is eighty years of age, nor to one whose wealth has been exhausted; if given to such, it will cause disease. It should be administered in all diseases to one who consumes ghee and eats wholesome food, to one who subsists on milk, or to a man devoted to *rasāyana* (rejuvenative therapy). Indeed, one should carry out the procedure for poison while prioritizing celibacy (*brahmacarya*). Having become healthy in mind through wholesome regimens, success is then beyond doubt.

Now, those for whom poison is not appropriate: it should not be given to one who is angry, nor to one afflicted by bile (pitta), nor to a eunuch, nor to one suffering from pulmonary consumption (rājayakṣman); nor to one engaged in labor due to hunger, thirst, fatigue, or travel, nor to one with wasting disease (kṣaya). Poison is not to be administered in the royal palace to pregnant women, children, or the elderly. Poison should never be given or consumed during a legal dispute. However, the preceptor may consume it to produce confidence in the disciple; even then, he should partake of pure poison only in the prescribed measure and not otherwise.

When taken according to the prescribed method, in the proper dose, at the right time, and by those who eat wholesome food, poison becomes a pacifier of all diseases and a nourisher of the vision for men. (67) [From the *Āyurvedīyagranthamālā*, Chapter on the Description of Poisonous Dosages: Now, the description of the dosage: If practiced starting from eight barley-corns up to the size of a sesame seed, purified poison becomes a remover of all diseases for men. (68) In the first stage, the dose is one mustard seed; in the second, two mustard seeds.

On the third, fourth, and likewise the fifth day, and on the sixth and seventh as well, one should increase the dose according to a progressive scale. One should carry through the first week with a dose the size of seven mustard seeds. In the second week, the poison should be administered with a decreasing scale; in the third week, poison the size of a barley grain should be given progressively. Likewise, in the fourth week, it should be administered by alternating between increasing and decreasing scales.

When such habituation has been achieved, the best of physicians should stabilize [the patient] as desired and then cause the cessation [of the dose]. This sequence of diminishing the administration is called the "poison-procedure" (*viṣakalpa*). One who is healthy should swallow a dose the size of a barley grain (*yava*), while one suffering from skin disease (*kuṣṭha*) should take a dose the size of a chickpea (*caṇaka*). In this manner, one may increase up to eight [barley grains], but the dose must not exceed that. Now, the wholesome foods (*pathya*) for poison: ghee, milk, sugar, honey, wheat, rice, and barley.

Black pepper, rock salt, grapes, sweet drinks, and cold [substances]; celibacy, a cool region, a cool time, and cool water—a wise man who consumes poison should resort to these. Now, regarding the examination of poison: when a mortal, through negligence, consumes an excessive dose of poison, then these stages (vegas) arise for that embodied being. In the first stage there is numbness; in the second, trembling occurs.

In the third stage there is a burning sensation, and in the fourth, a falling down to the ground. Thus the Āyurveda is revealed. In the fifth stage one vomits foam, while in the sixth there is indeed a state of impairment; in the seventh stage there is stupor, and in the eighth, death occurs. Having recognized these stages of the poison's onset, one should destroy it with mantras and medicinal substances, as long as the human being has not reached the eighth stage. When [poison] has been consumed in excessive measure, one should induce vomiting by that means.

One should administer goat’s milk until purgation occurs. When the goat’s milk has become stabilized within the abdomen of the person, the skilled physician should know that the force of the poison has been overcome. (Regarding verse 82, some read "tadā jīrṇam" [then it is digested]). The juice of *rajanī* and *meghanāda*, when drunk, destroys poison; likewise, *sarvāṅkṣī* or *ṭaṅkaṇa* with ghee is a supreme remover of poison. These are four formulations. Or, *putrajīvaka* or goat’s milk drunk with the water of *nimbu* [is effective].

It surely destroys the force of poison, just as rain extinguishes a forest fire. (84) The Vandhyakarkaṭī, when consumed with cow’s ghee, removes poison and venom; likewise, Trimūlī and Surabhijihvā pacify all poisons. (85) When food has been eaten in excessive measure, one should then drink ghee with ṭaṅkaṇa; by that means, the force of the poison will certainly and swiftly meet its destruction. (86) Vāgbhaṭa says: First, for one who has undergone emesis and purgation, [one should administer] Haridrā, Kaṭabhī, and jaggery.

One should employ *sindhuvāraka*, *niṣpāva*, *bāṣpikā*, *śataparvikā*, the roots of *taṇḍulīyaka*, *kukkuṭāṇḍa*, and *avalguja* for nasal drops (*nāvana*), collyrium (*añjana*), and internal potions (*pāna*) to pacify poison. To one who has consumed poison, one should give pure iron powder, as well as fine copper dust mixed with honey at the appropriate time; this cleanses the heart (*hṛdviśodhana*). Once the heart is purified, one should then cause a *śāṇa* measure of gold powder to be administered.

Poison does not cling to it, just as water does not cling to a golden vessel or a lotus leaf. A long life is produced even by means of a potent poison; this is the ritual prescribed for the benefit of practitioners, having issued from the mouth of Sadāśiva. I shall now proclaim the mantra which quickly destroys all poisons.

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Śrīghoṇe! Hara 2, dara 2, para 2, vara 2, vadha 2, lara 2, lo 2, hara 2, bhāṃ 2, sara 2, śa 2, kṣava 2, kṣī 2, hī 2! O Blessed One, Śrīghoṇe! Yaḥ 3, saḥ 3, vara 2, yaṃ saṃ 4! O you of the form of Khaṇḍāvara, hī 3! O excellent bird, speak of the security and well-being for humans! O Śekhara, rakhaḥ! Svāhā! By the mere recitation of this mantra, the Guhyakas and other spirits are destroyed. One should sprinkle that which is afflicted by poison with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times.

92 || He rises up with speed; one should restrain him by binding his crest-lock. If Śakra, empowered by the three mantras, should sound a drum, || 93 || then by that sound reaching across the distance, he renders [the victim] poisonless in an instant. Shake, shake! Quickly! Tremble, tremble! Possess, possess! Haḥ Ṭhaḥ Rahe! Homage to the glorious Garuḍa! Thus.

14 || Āyurvedaprakāśa || 197 || The knower of mantras should cause one who has lost consciousness to drink a mere handful of water over which this mantra has been recited seven times. By this, one struck by the force of poison from snakes and the like shall immediately become free of poison. (96) If the water should not be drunk, it must be administered three times; then, indeed, sprinklings of that water should be performed upon the chest. Alternatively, the wise one should strike him on the head with the forefinger. (97)

By reciting this mantra three times preceded by the syllable *matra*, one becomes free from poison in an instant. Now follows the mantra for removing the venom of a scorpion: *Oṃ kālo vicha kartarīyālo sonānī caॉca rūpāno patroro bichū utare to utāru na to garuḍamo haṃkāru āvego mora khāvego toḍa bichu vinare to hāka halolā kare merī bhakti gurukī śakti phuro matra*. The Lord said: "By means of this mantra, the knower of mantras, holding ashes in his hand, [should apply it]."

By reciting the mantra seven times or three times while wiping [the area], one makes a man bitten by a scorpion immediately free from poison; or by wiping with a peacock feather and the like, one shall destroy the poison. Now follows another mantra for removing the poison of a scorpion: *namo punapuro*. By wiping with the breath of the mouth, the knower of the ritual should draw three straight lines on the ground for himself using this urine. (99–101)

Facing those [venoms], one should make them straight by means of the mantra; making them so, one should repeatedly neutralize the poison through the repetition of the mantra twenty-one times. (102) [The two mantras previously experienced. Now, *arka*, *sehuṇḍa*, *dhattūra*, *lāṅgalī*, *karavīraka*, *guñjā*, and *ahi-phenā*—these are the seven types of secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*). (103) [From the *Āyurvedīya-granthamālā*, Chapter 198: A son crushed by these becomes "one with severed wings" (*chinnapakṣa*).

Happiness arises for him, and he swallows the *dhātus* (bodily constituents) in an instant. (104) The juice of *arka*, *sehuṇḍa*, and others may be used in formulations; or else, the juice derived from the limbs of an animal may be employed. (105) Another version: *arka*, *nugu*, *aṅgalī*, *guñjā*, *hārī*, *viṣamuṣṭi*, *āphnā*, *unmatta*, *jepāla*, and the nine species of fresh poisons (*navauṣaviṣajāti*). (106) *Bhaṅgā*, however, is not fixed [in its application], like *ajāyī* in the group of months (*māsagaṇa*).

Now, the purification of *lāṅgalī*: it attains purity by remaining in cow’s urine for one day. Thus ends the purification of *lāṅgalī*. Guñjā attains purity after being soaked in sour gruel (*kāñjika*) for one *prahara*. Thus ends the [discussion of] pure and impure substances. A handful of *viṣamuṣṭi* is purified when slightly fried in clarified butter (*ājya*). Thus ends the purification of *viṣamuṣṭi*. The *jepāla* (seed-pod), stripped of its skin and stalks, and known by those skilled in the essence of substances, is placed in buffalo dung for three days; then, cleansed with warm water, it is ground in a mortar along with *vāsā*.

Lapis lazuli (jepāla), when rubbed against new earthen plates until it becomes free of oil and resembles dust, and then repeatedly treated with lime-juice, becomes pure and rich in its qualities. Thus ends the purification of lapis lazuli. Datura seeds, having been soaked in cow’s urine for four watches (yāmas) and then dehusked and freed from their husks, should be employed in formulations once they are purified. Thus ends the purification of datura seeds. Opium, processed seven times with the juice of ginger, becomes pure; one should employ it according to the prescribed rules in the aforementioned formulations.

110 || Thus ends the purification of *ahi-phenā* (serpent-foam). As Caraka stated: "In the case of goats and sheep, [the purity] is uncertain because they graze on mixed [forbidden] fodder. (199) (14 || *Āyurvedaprakāśa*: Having steamed *bhaṅgā* with a decoction of *babbūla* and *baka*, one should dry it. After giving it an infusion (*bhāvanā*) of cow’s milk, when dried, one may employ it everywhere. 111 || Thus ends the purification of *bhaṅgā*. Now, for *viṣa-taila* (poison-oil): One should extract the essence of poison using a glass apparatus (*kācayantra*), just like the essence of *agaru*.

By that [process], oil and mercury become intoxicating; that indeed becomes a great hunger-inducer (kṣutkārī). In this manner, one should extract oil from dhattūra seeds and other sources according to the prescribed method. One should employ it in every formulation according to the stated measure, and not otherwise. Now, regarding the preparation of the poison-destroying mercury: take equal parts of raṅga, viṣa, ṭaṅkaṇa, mūṣaṇa, and tuttha. Having ground them with the juice of devadālī, the resulting mercury, when applied like a poison, becomes the sole destroyer of all poisons.

This *niṣka* (gold) restores life when applied by means of the *brusūtra* method in every respect; likewise, it [neutralizes] poison agitated by *jaṭā*, as well as other poisons seen to have been pulverized and administered to a patient. *Raṅga* is tin ash. Thus ends the section on mercury (*rasa*) regarding the removal of poison. Now, the varieties of salt: One should grind pure *sudhānidhi* (lime), thoroughly mixed with *pāśupata* (a type of mineral), along with mercury (*sūta*) containing metallic ores, and coated with *khaṭī*; one should then seal this within a crucible (*saṃpuṭa*).

Having ignited a fire beneath that salt which is situated inside [the crucible], one should forcibly extract the ash lying on top, which is as white as the moon or the kunda flower; this should be done slowly. Those who consume two grains of this, together with cloves, in the morning, purge repeatedly throughout the three watches of the night. This should be drunk with cool water. It destroys poison for a year—whether six-monthly or monthly—and even the instantaneous venom arising from mountains, extracted by the crooked claws of the king of beasts.

The *pāṃśupaṭu* salt is produced from the ash of *khārī* wood. It should be ground separately with cow’s urine and cow’s milk. It is also ground with mercury (*sūta*). It is extracted from the curved mane of the king of beasts—that is, it is produced from the lion's whiskers. This is the procedure for this "nectar-treasury" (*sudhānidhi*) salt, which destroys all poisons and breaks down other salts. Now, regarding the preparation of alkali (*kṣāra*): one should ignite the dry wood of an alkaline tree in a fire.

Having taken that ash and quickly placed it in an earthen vessel with four times as much water, one should stir it and let it settle overnight; in the morning, one should take the clear water. That water should be boiled over a fire until it is completely dried up. Then, having removed it from the vessel, the white-colored alkaline residue should be collected. It may be used as a powder for rubbing or drunk when dissolved in a decoction. Thus, the wise man should employ these two types of alkali in the prescribed procedures. This concludes the preparation of alkali.

Thus ends the chapter on the treatment of poisons, artificial poisons, and the like, in the *Āyurvedaprakāśa* composed by Bhaiṣajyavaidya, an ornament of the illustrious Upādhyāya Sārakhata family and a resident of Kāśī.
